in writing. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on the content of her report. construction is an equally sensitive and important area of the european economy and we need harmonisation. i say sensitive not only in terms of how the sector has responded to the crisis, but also in terms of the large number of workers, 12 million, and smes, some 65 000. i strongly support the idea that we must recognize the need for a high level of occupational safety and health in construction. i am equally and clearly referring to accidents at work, which are quite common, but also to the dangerous substances used in the process. in conclusion, i would add one thing: the single market in construction needs support in accordance with its importance and specificity, but also for the sensitive aspects i mentioned at the beginning of my speech.
the european commission has started the process of concluding voluntary partnership agreements with countries that export wood to the european union. in this context, i believe it is important to develop a structure of active participation of local communities, both to monitor the implementation of the agreement and to improve the governance framework in the forestry sector and, not least, to avoid corruption as much as possible. the involvement of civil society in the process of drafting the agreement with cameroon is a positive signal in this regard. at the same time, concrete measures are needed to continue this type of dialogue in all signatory countries. the building of a socially and environmentally sustainable timber industry, including by reducing deforestation and forest degradation in these countries, should also be pursued. the agreements must respect the european union's international commitments on the environment and sustainable development.
in writing. flegt voluntary partnership agreements were a good basis on which to build international cooperation to tackle the problem of deforestation. and they continue to show their relevance today, especially in the context of last year's illegal timber regulation. countries which adhere to such voluntary schemes are able to give certain guarantees about the legality and environmental sustainability of their timber sources. there are clear benefits in terms of environmental protection, although we should be mindful of the fact that trade in legally harvested timber is not necessarily sensitive to needs of indigenous people. it is important that, as more vpas are agreed, their effects are closely monitored and that their terms take full account of the needs and human rights of people who are dependent on forests, but who often do not have a voice in the management of those forests.
the current interim partnership agreement concluded in november 2007 by the european commission and the states of papua new guinea and fiji has been strongly criticised by civil society and politicians in the pacific region. they underlined the negative consequences that the agreement had on the level of interregional solidarity and the political will for economic integration in the region. the latter was divided into groups which negotiated individually and under pressure to reach an interim agreement with the european commission. it is also considered that the granting of originating status, a derogation from the payment of customs duties in the union for fishery products originating in papua new guinea and fiji, has led to the creation of a processing centre for these products, including non-originating products, by firms in the neighbouring states, with the aim of taking advantage of the derogation. this would have a detrimental effect on industry, workers and local incomes, given that the fishing industry is one of the most important job generators in these countries. it would also represent unfair competition for european products. it is therefore possible that the agreement had the opposite of the desired effect. the european commission must therefore ensure that the future partnership agreement will contribute both to the development of a sustainable, job-creating local fisheries industry and to closer regional integration, for example by negotiating the future agreement with the pacific region as a whole.
i appreciate the interest of my colleagues in the italian delegation in the situation of abandoned children, an interest which we all share, but this is a matter for national jurisdiction only. i insisted on taking part in this debate because i come from a country that is under pressure to resume international adoptions and to change the legislation in force. but in romania, there are more families willing to adopt than there are adoptable children, and our legislation, which has been attended by many international experts, is in perfect coordination with the european one. with reference to this resolution, i would point out that the phrase 'the right of the child to be internationally adopted', as provided for in paragraph (d), is not recognised by the un convention and the hague convention. international adoption is only one option. these children are brought into the system because of the precarious situation of the families from which they come, which, according to the law and international conventions, should not be a reason for adoption. hence the high number of children in the foster care system. 22,966 children have a parent, though. romanian law does not provide for parental deprivation except in the case of abuse. so these kids aren't in any position to be adopted. so are the 22,285 children in foster care. the reasoning behind the resolution must be focused on the best interests of the child, as my colleagues have said before, and not the adopter. it is the duty of each state and no one else to choose the best solutions for its children. finally, i recommend that everyone should become more familiar with national legislation. i am referring to the fact that, for example, several italian juvenile courts issued seven adoption decisions for romanian children in 2009, without taking into account our legislation.
i welcome this debate in the european parliament's plenary, on the premise that the protection of children's rights is and must be a priority for every member state of our union. the ultimate goal for everyone here is to promote the interests of children. of course, common and strict criteria, which the member states must implement, are necessary to improve the care and living conditions of institutionalized and abandoned children and to protect them when they are adopted, and especially now, when budgetary austerity seems to be the only idea of the right-wing governments in the european union. the first step is therefore to ensure that these children are properly cared for; the second is to combat child trafficking and child prostitution; the third is to remember that, in the interests of children, priority must be given to adoptions by a family member and national adoptions; and the fourth is to give priority to international adoptions. because here we can only draw conclusions from the past, opening the gates for intentional adoptions in romania meant the creation of unprecedented child trafficking networks, cases of child abduction and their sale to the west, in collaboration with european and international organizations. between 1997 and 2000, romania exported 9,150 copies, and my country will never accept such a monstrosity again. finally, i would like to ask you, through you, to ask commissioner reding to clarify the allegations that have appeared in the romanian and international media regarding the european agency for the supervision of intercountry adoptions, a proposal that also appears in the study commissioned by the european commission. a colleague in the european parliament is still awaiting commissioner reding's answer to a question.
the oral question which launched the resolution on intercountry adoptions brings a subject of major importance to the european parliament's agenda. international adoption can only be considered as an alternative means once national adoption arrangements have been exhausted. intercountry adoption also presents a number of particularities and difficulties, which are largely due to the limited interaction between the child and the adopters in the period prior to adoption and the problems of linguistic and cultural adaptation encountered by the child after adoption. the principle of the best interests of the child and not of the adopter, as enshrined in the un convention and the hague convention, must underpin the european parliament's resolution, focusing on the development of the child in a family environment, ensuring continuity in the child's upbringing and taking into account the child's ethnic, religious, cultural and linguistic background. the principle of reintegration of the child from the protection system into the biological or extended family is essential in the analysis of the adoption case and the drafting of the resolution. i would like to draw attention to a confusion that is often made between the number of children separated from their parents but in the foster care system and the number of children who are available for adoption. separated children enjoy limited protection from the state and are not adoptable. i believe that we do not need control mechanisms and that the existing principles at international level relating to them are sufficient.
i would also like to refer to the un convention which states that international adoptions can only be an alternative to helping a child when he cannot be found a foster family or when he cannot be properly cared for in his country of origin. the risks of liberalizing international adoptions are many. on the one hand, the possibility of child trafficking and abuse is increasing due to financial interests and the difficulties in monitoring the post-adoption situation. on the other hand, separating a child from his biological parents, from his place of origin, can have dire psychological, social, and educational consequences. when we talk about adoption, we must first of all have in mind the welfare of the child and therefore we must not put pressure on the member states of the union, with their different traditions and legal procedures in the field of adoption, to liberalize international adoptions.
the resolution on intercountry adoption in the union should clearly mention the following: families intending to use intercountry adoption must have the opinion of the competent national institution in their country of origin; the international adoption must take place only under the responsibility of the competent authorities of the two member states, of the family and of the child. the monitoring of children adopted through the intercountry adoption procedure should also be carried out by the national institution with responsibilities in this field. last but not least, the competent national authorities should report regularly to the member state of origin of the child adopted through the intercountry adoption procedure on the development of the child.
the agenda includes one-minute speeches on matters of political importance.
the use of psychotropic and psychoactive substances, which are usually in the grey area of legislation, has far more harmful effects than any other known drug. these substances are commonly found in european dream shops and are known as ethnobotanics, a term coined to give a harmless appearance to drug trafficking and use. countries such as poland, israel, sweden, denmark, england, germany have already banned a significant number of substances identified as psychotropic and psychoactive. the substances on the market, although not on the list of banned substances, are very difficult to control, making it impossible for the medical profession to help because the chemical combinations used have unknown reactions. the only measure that can be taken is to ban the operation of these stores, after which we must concentrate our efforts on eliminating marketing via the internet.
the agenda includes the report by daciana octavia sârbu, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the recognition of agriculture as a strategic sector for food security [2010/2112 (ini) ].
the reporter. − i am honoured to present my report, which speaks to the strategic importance of agriculture in ensuring food security in the european union. agriculture is neglected in the debate on the eu's strategy and future, and the report shows that europe is not food secure, that farmers and entire rural areas are in danger of disappearing, and that new challenges such as climate change are threatening to destabilise already dwindling food supplies, not only in europe but also in the world. with food production set to increase by at least 70% by 2050 to meet the global food needs, food security needs to be at the centre of both global and european debates. the european union must respond firmly to these challenges, and through this report we are trying to propose today some concrete ways of acting. first, we need a strong common agricultural policy designed to guarantee the food security of its citizens and to contribute to global food security in the context of limited resources and the effects of climate change. we cannot talk about food security without addressing two key issues: market and price volatility and dwindling global food supplies. as regards price volatility, i asked the commission to strengthen the role of market intervention instruments in the new cap and to take more substantial measures to limit speculation on agricultural markets. today, global food supplies are much more limited than in the past, with estimates that they can supply the world's food needs for only a month and a half. i therefore thought it would be beneficial to create a global food reserve system, both emergency food reserves to reduce hunger and food reserves to be used to regulate prices on agricultural markets, under international auspices and drawing on the expertise of existing institutions such as the un or the fao. another important issue addressed in this report is the situation of young farmers. if we are thinking about the future of european agriculture, then we must pay more attention to young farmers. at european level, only 7% of farmers are under 35. i have therefore asked the commission to provide for measures to encourage them. on the other hand, we stressed the need to preserve the diversity of european agriculture. in this context, i mentioned that traditional agricultural practices, family farms, small farms and organic farming can make a valuable contribution to food security and called for the creation of programmes at european level to support these types of agriculture. but let us not forget that poverty and hunger still exist in the union and that millions of europeans have been receiving european food aid this winter. in the context of the economic crisis, it is therefore of the utmost importance to maintain the european programme 'food aid for the most deprived' with european funding. in conclusion, i would like to thank the shadow rapporteurs and the other colleagues on the committee on agriculture for their good cooperation and contributions to the drafting of this report, and the secretariat of the committee on agriculture, and i hope that together we will adopt tomorrow a report that meets the expectations of the european citizens.
in writing. the increase in global food demand as a result of the world's growing population is clearly reflected in natural food resources and involves new regulations and precautions in the area of food security. the eu has a priority mission to guarantee the right to food security for its member states and to support developing countries in achieving an adequate level of food security. it considers it important to promote the production and marketing of traditional local foods. regional food has multiple benefits: reduced transport costs and reduced risk of perishability. there are many regions with a strong agricultural potential that is not being exploited because of social or economic imbalances, such as the increasing ageing of the rural population or industrialization. thus, large areas of agricultural land are not used efficiently. regional authorities can play a key role in ensuring food security by supporting the agricultural capacity of regions with this potential. the eu is one of the world leaders in research and innovation, including in agriculture. with a growing majority of the urban population, a new challenge arises: how much priority is given to the development of urban agriculture in order to ensure food security through various models such as vertical urban agriculture?

in writing. there is currently too much uncertainty about access to healthcare, reimbursement and responsibility for clinical supervision in cross-border healthcare. this directive allows all patients - not just the best informed or the wealthiest among them - to benefit from a number of rights already recognised by the court of justice of the european union in relation to healthcare. the organisation and management of social security systems are the sole responsibility of the member states. the proposal concerns patients and their mobility within the eu, not the free movement of service providers. the directive provides for cooperation between member states in particular as regards the recognition of medical recommendations (treatments, prescriptions, etc.) issued in another member state, ehealth and hta (high technology assessment). citizens' access to this information will be facilitated through the reference network, established from the national contact points. the romanian authorities must therefore ensure that its citizens have access to information. the adoption of this report helps to ensure a good balance between the rights of eu patients to access the best medical treatment and the protection of the financial sustainability of the national social security system.
member of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, first allow me to pay tribute to parliament, in particular to the rapporteur, mrs matias, for your commitment to addressing alzheimer’s and other dementias. the commission fully shares your concern. dementia means great suffering for millions of europeans and their families. with a population ageing fast, now is the time for europe to act. this is why the commission put forward a communication on alzheimer’s and other dementias in 2009 with action to improve prevention and diagnosis, research and best practice exchange. i am delighted that parliament is supporting ongoing work in this context and presenting a comprehensive set of recommendations. this report and its recommendations are very timely at a moment when the commission is about to launch a joint action with the member states on alzheimer’s in april, the so-called alcove (alzheimer cooperative valuation in europe). i am persuaded that this joint action will deliver on many of the recommendations that you are adopting here today. the joint action will focus on prevention – an area which parliament underlines in this report – and also on improving knowledge and data and sharing good practices. it will also address another area where parliament is calling for action: the rights of people living with dementia. i agree with you that we need fully coordinated research to understand better how to prevent or delay the onset of dementia. this is why the commission has launched a joint programming initiative on combating neurodegenerative diseases, in particular alzheimer’s. for the first time, 23 countries are working together to tackle alzheimer’s. there are good practices across europe on diagnosis and treatment for alzheimer’s and the commission is fostering exchange of knowledge and good practice. as recommended by parliament, i can also confirm that the innovation union initiative under the europe 2020 strategy will take as its first pilot area for the new european innovation partnership the topic of active and healthy ageing. action to support people suffering from dementia could be developed in this context. a good example could be the ongoing parliament initiative on carers. we hope to be able to support further innovative actions in this area which may also address the issues of alzheimer’s and other dementias. finally the commission looks favourably at a number of other recommendations, including declaring 2014 as european year of the brain. let me assure you that the commission is committed to doing its share to address dementia. let me now address the second topic in this debate: the petition filed by mr klein, the inventor and producer of the inhaler ‘effecto’. the placing on the market of the device in question was originally refused in germany in 1997. this decision was not pursued further, either by the commission, the german authorities, or the manufacturer. the then distributor indicated at the time that it would conduct further studies before placing the product on the market again. the device was placed back on the market in 2002 under a new name. when the product was again prohibited by the german authorities in 2005, the commission carefully analysed the case and concluded the procedure by formal letter to the german authorities and the manufacturer in july 2007. the commission analysis was that the prohibition by the german authorities was justified because the clinical data provided by the manufacturer was insufficient to demonstrate the safety of the device. according to the medical device directive, safety has to be demonstrated by the manufacturer in order for him to be allowed to use the ce marking. this meant that the applicable legal provision was article 18 of the directive which addresses cases where a product is placed on the market with improperly affixed ce marking. in this case, there is no formal commission decision. since, in the commission’s view, the case is not one to which the safeguard clause procedure applies, it has no reason to request notification of the 2005 prohibition adopted by the german authorities. the obstacle which the petitioner faces in placing the product on the market is the decision of the german authorities (the 2005 prohibition) and not a decision of the commission. the petitioner had clear legal avenues which he could pursue at national level, and indeed he has made use of these opportunities. his claims, however, were rejected by the german courts. i would like to stress that the commission has, since 2007, invited the petitioner to bring the device into compliance by providing the missing clinical data and has facilitated contacts between him and the german authorities to that end. to the commission’s knowledge, no action has been taken by the petitioner so far.
on behalf of the epp group. i'm going to talk about alzheimer's and other dementias. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs matias, on her work and, as the shadow rapporteur for the epp group on this dossier, i would also like to thank all the colleagues who have contributed. the attention paid to this file shows the importance of the subject and, at the same time, the gravity of the phenomenon. the number of people with dementia stands at 9.9 million, with alzheimer's disease accounting for the largest proportion, and we expect this number to rise dramatically by 2020, with the disease still underdiagnosed in the european union. there are inequalities between member states in prevention, access to treatment and care. the actions are fragmented, the reactions are uneven in terms of research and the fight against this disease. the report is an important step towards the fight against this disease in the european union and a key step towards introducing a new way of working together among member states to take coordinated action to tackle problems affecting europe as a whole. the report supports solidarity between countries, the exchange of good practices, to avoid duplication of effort and waste of resources. i want to emphasize the importance of preventive diagnosis and early intervention in the early stages of the disease, and i believe this is the key to progress in the fight against this disease. i would also like to stress the importance of a multidisciplinary approach to research in this area. the fragmentation of disciplines and the weak link between primary, clinical, public health and social research influence the transfer of scientific findings into medical practice and care provision. the fact that all this is done at national level accentuates fragmentation. therefore, we need to focus on the multidisciplinary approach and on the transfer of findings and knowledge at the community level.
today, there is still much uncertainty and unknown about alzheimer's disease, and unfortunately, the situation continues to worsen as the population in europe ages. we obviously need more research and more studies on the causes and treatment of dementia, but as with noncommunicable diseases, there is evidence that simple lifestyle measures can prevent many conditions. that is why, in the amendments tabled, i have called for more research to be done into the effects of nutrition on the development of alzheimer's disease. many of us surely know at least one person affected by this disease or another form of dementia, and we know that, in fact, the personal costs are far greater than the social or financial costs. the widespread and devastating effects of dementia on so many people are of concern to us all. as a result, we have a very comprehensive report containing all the key issues and we want a positive reaction from the commission but also from the member states.
in writing. data on the prevalence of alzheimer' s disease and other dementias are available in the european union countries and have been collected by alzheimer europe. alzheimer's disease has been and is the leading cause of dementia in all countries. it accounts for 74.5% of dementia cases in north america, 61.4% in europe and 46.5% in asia. however, there are cases of undiagnosed alzheimer's disease in the european union, according to the latest available epidemiological data, only half of the people suffering from this disease are currently identified. in this context, i believe that member states need to develop long-term policies and action plans to improve access to funding for research into dementia and alzheimer's disease, including prevention research, at a level commensurate with their economic impact on society, and that anticipate and prevent social and demographic trends and focus on supporting the families of patients who care for them, thus providing social protection to vulnerable people with dementia.
member of the commission. − mr president, the commission welcomes the financial times’s scrutiny as it represents an important contribution to opening and broadening public debate about the efficiency and effectiveness of cohesion policy. the commission is aware of the habitually slower take-up at the beginning of a programming period. however, the most recent data show that the commission made more cohesion policy payments in the fourth quarter of 2010 than ever before. the vast majority of the payments made were interim payments, i.e. reimbursements of expenditure already made and certified in the member states. thus it is certain that, as has been seen in previous programming periods, cohesion policy spending is accelerating. absorption rates, in terms of eu payments to member states, are now at 21% for the cohesion fund, 22% for the european regional development fund (erdf) and 23% for the european social fund (esf). as regards support provided to multinational and large companies, the commission would emphasise that a primary objective of cohesion policy is growth and the creation of new jobs for particular regions and member states. any support for productive investment has to be seen in that context. promoting job creation and economic growth can be achieved in many ways, from setting-up small enterprises to supporting larger companies. cohesion policy intervention supports productive investment that is primarily targeted at small and medium-sized enterprises, as specified by the erdf and esf regulations. the commission also stressed the role of small and medium-sized enterprises during negotiation of the current programming documents. the vast majority of productive investment and investment in the development of endogenous potential is targeted at smes. however, there may be cases where, in line with the regulations, co-financing is granted to larger companies subject to compliance with the objectives of the funds and programmes concerned. in total, cohesion policy has allocated some eur 55 billion to business support between 2007 and 2013, a large share of which supports innovation in smes. the commission would like to point out that multinationals are not beneficiaries of the support extended by the esf. workers receive the co-financed training. the esf supports people. it is about providing training and retraining and improving skills to prepare people and help them find a job. a worker who has been employed in a given enterprise may well then find himself or herself engaged in another company. therefore, what matters is the skill capital that workers manage to build to sustain their inclusion in the labour market, not the name or type of enterprises providing the training. the commission considers that, from a policy perspective, firms should not receive european funding for investments which would lead to the loss of employment by the same company in another region of the european union, because the net effect of the esf investment might be zero or even negative. in cases where a company which has received cohesion policy support closes down, or ceases to support a project, within five years – or three years in the case of smes – this funding needs to be paid back. my final point – but it is a crucial one – is that while there are clearly areas for improvement this cannot and should not overshadow the major positive impact that cohesion policy is having. i would like to assure you that the commission is not shying away from the problems. indeed, in the past we have proposed changes, some of which were taken up, and we will continue to drive improvement of cohesion policy. cohesion policy brings clear benefits to the poorer regions of the european union, but it also clearly benefits the rest of europe.
i would also like to thank the commissioner for the quality of the information he has given, but i would like to add a comment: in a debate like this, when we are dealing with a subject like this, i think we should rather focus on future measures to avoid similar situations and, if i may say so, perhaps even more importantly, ask ourselves whether such reports, once they have come to the attention of the public, are not in any way likely to reduce citizens' confidence in the work of the european institutions.

on behalf of the s&d group one year after the tragedy that devastated haiti, as you said, the reconstruction process has not met the expectations of the people and the commitments made by the international community. moreover, the efforts to rebuild the state seem, in the light of the revolutions of the past few months, to have reached a dead end. ravaged by an earthquake and struck by a cholera epidemic blamed on the un blue helmets, the country also plunged into a serious political crisis. i think there are three plans for the haitian crisis that we need to act on in the next period, otherwise the efforts so far risk being compromised. it is necessary to announce the results of the investigation into the causes of the cholera epidemic as soon as possible, to calm the anger of the population against the un presence. secondly, the extension of the interim period which will be triggered by the end of president préval's mandate on 7 february must be avoided, and new elections, under close international supervision, are the only viable and democratic solution. finally, i believe that this moment of balance must mark a turning point in the reconstruction efforts, undermined by inefficiency, delays and conflicting interests of some countries in the region. let us not forget that of the $10 billion pledged at the new york donors conference in march 2010, only $1.2 billion has been disbursed so far, with the european union's effort accounting for a significant share. to the concern for solving the problems of the million haitians surviving in the emergency camps, where poverty, misery and sexual violence are reaching worrying proportions, we owe it to add the long-term perspective of sustainable investment in haiti and concrete support for the construction of a viable state structure.
on january 12, 2010, the haitian state was literally smashed, as several of my colleagues have said; now, a year after this terrible earthquake, reconstruction is still pending. in the meantime, the cholera epidemic, the elections, all of these complicated matters. port-au-prince is actually a huge refugee camp today. the haitian people are only surviving because of the efforts of humanitarian organizations. we should be grateful to these organizations. as the united nations special representative for this country said, haiti has become a republic of ngos. but how long can this situation last? we see that the health situation is catastrophic, the reconstruction of the education system is absolutely necessary, the process of rebuilding after the disaster, all of this evokes the need for a reconstruction of the haitian state. beyond the earthquake, the absence of institutions and good governance is very problematic today. the efforts must therefore focus on restoring the capacity of the state and on building democracy in haiti. the need for a credible and transparent electoral process, with a view to the second round of elections in february, must be emphasised very strongly. in conclusion, i would like to say that the reconstruction of haiti must be done, if i may, otherwise. 'otherwise' means that reconstruction must be done better than before, to prevent similar disasters from happening again. "otherwise" means that our rebuilding efforts must involve, i would say, local communities. i think the main stakeholders, the haitians, need to be consulted in this reconstruction process.
one year after the devastating earthquake in haiti, the concrete results of the reconstruction process are still not visible. the blockade is mainly due to the fact that the haitian state does not have the capacity to provide basic public services by its own means. the political will is lacking and the haitian authorities are failing to implement decisions aimed at reconstruction. this makes it considerably more difficult for the interim reconstruction commission, the main body responsible for the effective management of the resources released by the international community, to function. this situation will continue unless political stabilization of the country, restoration of state capacity and appointment of a functioning government is achieved. i therefore believe that the eu must make every effort to support a legitimate and transparent electoral process. the correct conduct of the second round of elections, scheduled for february, is the only way to end the political crisis.

in writing. − i voted in favour of the european parliament's resolution on international adoption in the european union, based on the romanian experience in this field. it is indeed necessary to analyse all national adoption systems, to see what their strengths and weaknesses are, and to recommend best practices for adoption by member states. it would be a real step forward to coordinate policies and strategies at european level on the instrument for intercountry adoption, with a view to improving assistance in the field of information services, intercountry adoption preparation, processing of applications for intercountry adoption and post-adoption services, so that the right of orphaned and abandoned children to have a family and to be protected becomes effective.
in writing. − the cessation of international adoptions was one of the conditions for romania's accession to the european union. romania decided in 2001 to impose a moratorium on the ban on intercountry adoptions after the european parliament's rapporteur for romania, baroness emma nicholson, condemned the cases of child trafficking and criticized the romanian state for neglecting children. i believe that priority should be given, whenever possible and in the best interests of the child, to adoption in the child's country of origin as an alternative solution, which could be the finding of a foster family, personal or residential care or the finding of a family through international adoption, in accordance with relevant national legislation and international conventions, and that institutional placement should be used only as a temporary solution. it is also important to establish a methodological framework at european level to ensure that the development of the adopted child in his or her new family is assessed through periodic post-adoption reports drawn up by the social services of the state to which the adopted child has arrived and transmitted to the competent authorities of the state from which the child has been adopted. this mechanism should be achieved through coordination of actions between member states, the ec, in cooperation with the hague conference, the council of europe and child protection organisations to prevent trafficking of children for adoption.
in writing. − serbia has received an encouragement: the vote on the stabilisation and association agreement; and i hope that the ratification process will be accelerated by the vote in the european parliament today. i note that one of the problems raised in the report on the stabilisation and association agreement is related to serbia's non-recognition of the kosovo authorities and the maintenance of parallel structures. romania has not recognised kosovo's independence, which was unilaterally declared in violation of international law. serbia is a very good neighbour of romania, with which we are linked by centuries of history, and romania understands how to support its friends. it is clear that serbia's future is in europe and its cooperation with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia should demonstrate belgrade's commitment to european values, democracy and human rights. obviously serbia will have to follow the same path as all member states to join, but it must enjoy equal treatment in this respect. the latest developments have shown that serbia has understood what the european community expects of it. visible progress has been made and the eu must tactfully address some aspects of belgrade's recent history that are weighing on the serbian people.
in writing. − the european union is based on principles such as reconciliation and peaceful coexistence, with the same objectives of improving relations between the peoples of the region. in this context, i believe that serbia's future lies with the eu countries and i believe that serbia must step up its efforts in this direction.
in writing. - i voted for this report and this is not the first time i have spoken here about my reasons for doing so, including my own. the western balkans and serbia are not only an area of strategic interest for the union, it is not only the citizens of this area who need us. we all need them. the union is serbia's main trading partner and that says a lot. serbia has a unique situation in europe, it is the country with the largest number of refugees and displaced persons. i am convinced that the acceleration of serbia's integration process is beneficial for the entire western balkans region.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on the integration of serbia. one important reason is that serbia can become an important player in ensuring security and stability in the region. at the same time, constructive strategies on regional cooperation and good neighbourly relations are key elements of the stabilisation and association process. all of these are key factors in the process of transforming the western balkans into an area of long-term stability and sustainable development. serbia's eu integration process is also being encouraged by progress in the reform process. serbia's efforts in the field of minority protection are commendable, even if access to information and education in minority languages needs to be further improved, especially for the romanian minority, which has been severely discriminated against over the last century. progress in promoting gender equality is also remarkable, in particular the adoption of the gender equality act and the national action plan for the empowerment of women and the promotion of gender equality.
in writing. - i support the rapporteur and i voted in favour of her proposal. alzheimer's disease is becoming more common and affects more and more people, all the more so as the ratio between the working population and the retired population continues to decline. changes in behavior and personality make the sick dependent on others. what the rapporteur is proposing is better coordination between the member states, solidarity and support for the people affected, but also for those involved.
in writing. − alzheimer's disease strikes everywhere equally, and the fact that scientific progress has failed to diagnose it before it starts or to find a cure makes it all the more important to find solutions to improve the lives of those who suffer from it. over 8 million europeans suffer from neurodegenerative diseases and the prognosis is not encouraging in 30 years the number of patients will double. this calls for improved coordination between member states, as well as a more effective, more solidarity-based response to prevent and treat people affected by dementia, particularly alzheimer's, and to support those around them. for a european strategy in this area to be successful, all countries must give priority to the development of national action plans. we also need to focus on early diagnosis and prevention and on the collection and processing of epidemiological data on the disease. after these fundamental steps, integrated measures are needed from research to the provision of healthcare. it is important to address gaps in areas such as vocational training or family support and to work towards raising awareness of the problems associated with living with dementia.
in writing. − the adoption of the report on a european initiative on alzheimer's disease is an important step in the fight against the disease, given that the number of people in europe suffering from dementia is 9.9 million, with alzheimer's patients representing the largest proportion of the population. the adoption of this report will enable member states to take coordinated action to combat this disease in the european union. i see a potential solution in the efficient use of the resources of the europe 2020 'innovation union' pilot initiative and the 'healthy and active ageing pilot partnership', due to be launched this spring. given that the number of alzheimer's patients is expected to increase dramatically by 2020, it is necessary to develop both public-institutional partnerships and public-private partnerships in the implementation of research projects in the future, thus leveraging facilities, resources and expertise from both the private and public sectors to combat the effects of alzheimer's disease and other dementias.
in writing. − this report is a fundamental step towards the formulation of a european strategy in this area, based on four key objectives: promoting early diagnosis and quality of life; improving epidemiological knowledge of this disease and coordinating existing research; supporting solidarity between member states through the exchange of best practices; and respecting the rights of people affected by dementia and their carers. every year 1.4 million citizens living in europe develop some form of dementia. a new case is diagnosed every 24 seconds. nearly one in 20 people over 65 and one in five over 80 suffer from dementia. it is estimated that over 8 million europeans aged 30 to 99 suffer from neurodegenerative diseases (alzheimer's - half), and scientists predict a doubling of this number every 20 years. as there are inequalities in access to diagnosis and treatment, not only from one country to another but also within the same country, it is necessary to develop national action plans, focusing on solidarity oriented towards the prevention and treatment of people affected by dementia, in particular alzheimer's, and supporting the people around the patients (healthcare professionals, service providers or relatives).
in writing. − the situation in haiti has become very serious, as all the efforts of the international community have not led to an improvement in the situation of this state, devastated by civil war and natural disasters, now affected by a cholera epidemic. last year's devastating earthquake brought haiti into the world's public eye, but despite concerted efforts amid a wave of strong emotion, things are not looking good. that is why perhaps the most important part of the resolution adopted by the european parliament is the call to the un to reconsider the mandate of minustah in haiti, in the wake of the epidemic and the tensions generated by the recent elections, which are strongly contested domestically and whose fairness the international community has serious doubts about. the poor population of the small state is actually the big loser of all these problems. it is crucial that the un be and remain at the forefront of coordinating all civil and military operations, both to restore security and humanitarian aid and to rebuild and develop. the entire international community, and even more so the european union, must put its involvement in haiti's reconstruction at the top of its agenda before it is too late for its people.
in writing. − it is important for the people of haiti that the european union stands in solidarity with them following the catastrophe that has affected them, resulting in significant loss of life and material damage. i therefore welcome europe's decision to commit to helping financially the reconstruction process in this country with some 1.2 billion euros and the proposal of the eu high representative for foreign affairs, catherine ashton, to adopt an economic plan for the next 10 years, focusing also on development and growth in the area, in addition to the reconstruction of the country. it is an important decision, especially as the eu is one of the caribbean country's most important donors. however, i believe that community funds should be distributed on the basis of criteria similar to those applied in the member states, namely on the basis of concrete programmes for the reconstruction of houses, schools, roads and other infrastructure, as well as the granting of microcredit to stimulate the development and launch of micro-projects for economic recovery, following the model existing in the eu for micro-enterprises. after world war ii, the united states implemented the marshall plan, which was instrumental in the reconstruction of western europe. europe can launch a similar programme for haiti.
mr president, the plight of christians in the middle east, asia and africa is no accident. this is not a series of regrettable but uncoordinated attacks. on the contrary, it is classic mass persecution. the christians are intimidated, evicted or killed with a clear purpose: religious cleansing. this is happening as we here in europe are bending over backwards to accommodate the endless sensibilities of muslim believers. the result is a europe full of mosques and the middle east purged of christians. but this is not about numbers. it is about liberty and identity. even for those among us who do not believe, christianity should be more than a forgotten, exotic and diminishing sect. we are free to believe or not, but we are not free to see our freedoms abused. this approach means that we should make religious freedom a precondition in our relations with sovereign states. this approach should be inscribed into law and become part of the high representative’s mandate.
vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, i wanted, if i might, to pick up two or three of the many strands of ideas which have been given to me – first of all to thank honourable members and to recognise the strength of feeling and expression of support for some of the work that we are seeking to do in this area. as i have already indicated, part of the reason i was very pleased to be able to participate in this debate is that this has been raised once before with the foreign affairs council – but we will come back to it at the end of january – and the concerns that honourable members have made have resonated and echoed with the concerns which have been raised with me from a variety of different sources, not least from some of the member states and some of the ministers who have been most concerned about these issues. i want to make it clear that i did in fact talk about christianity. i began by expressing the reasons i had for specifically going to bethlehem, and that was to recognise that although i was in the middle east i was also in the heart, in a sense, of many religions – specifically on the eve of the orthodox christmas. that was a very powerful statement in itself and it was a very personal and deliberate act to do that. i know that, unfortunately, mr mauro is no longer in his place to hear my reply, but i hope that he is told that i did in my words indeed mention that. i want to just pick up two or three things. a number of honourable members have raised the question of how we use the tools that are available to us to ensure that these issues can be addressed. i want to remind honourable members that almost all of the trade and cooperation agreements which we have concluded since 1995 have included a human rights clause, and that exists in agreements with, i believe now, 134 countries. the principal purpose is to demonstrate the shared commitment to human rights which we have, but it also constitutes the legal basis for sanctions in the event of grave human rights violations. honourable members will remember that in my previous capacity it was i who raised the issue of ‘gsp plus’ and sri lanka. you will know that we have taken steps to suspend them from that scheme, specifically on the grounds of issues of human rights. it is very important, as honourable members have said, that we continue to look at the way in which we conclude agreements and the tools at our disposal to do that and to make sure that those levers are pulled if necessary. one of the things that i think will be very interesting as the commission begins to look at the future of the gsp regulation is to see whether aspects of that regulation that concern the ratification and implementation of human rights and conventions could be improved. i also wanted to put the other side of that, which is of course the instruments that we use to promote and support democracy in human rights. we are, as honourable members know, supporting projects worldwide in the fight against racism, xenophobia or discrimination on any ground. we have funded anti-discrimination ngos in some 60 countries. therefore, we strike a balance between using the tools at our disposal to ensure that we are able to demonstrate when we feel very strongly that this has been violated, and using those tools – combined with the willingness that we have and the availability that we have – to support those ngos, in particular those that are active in the field of anti-discrimination. i wanted also to just touch on one other area, and that is the role of the delegations across the world and the role of monitoring what is happening. a number of honourable members indeed raised this as a particular point. i have already said that i think it is really important that we monitor the issues across the world. i was particularly struck by one issue that honourable members talked about in a number of contributions and what, in a sense, has become very much more recognised in recent weeks and months but which nonetheless has been a concern to many honourable members for a very long time: the concern about the way in which religious people, of all kinds of religion, are treated or discriminated against on a regular basis across the world and our need to be mindful and watchful of those issues, not when they become violent – when they become violent in a sense we are of course bound to act – but before they become violent too, when this is a regular source of discrimination. i think it is important that we see our delegations across the world as a source of being able to see and recognise the kind of discrimination that honourable members feel ‘bubbles below the surface’, if i can use that expression, and notify us when they see it. i also think it is important, as i have indicated that we put forward at the last foreign affairs council, that in our human rights work and in the report that we produced we are also addressing the situation of religious minorities across the world. christianity has played a very important part in our discussions today but many honourable members have pointed out that this also needs to apply in ensuring that we have respect and tolerance for other faiths in everything that we do. i think it will be important to try and get a sense of what is really happening both through our monitoring in our reports and also through our delegations across the world. that i think will give us a greater sense of knowing how then to use the instruments that are available to us, particularly from the commission side; but also a sense of the political will, not just from me, but – as you have rightly pointed out – as parliamentarians you have a strong voice and a strong role in this, together with the member states and the ministers involved in the member states. as i began, i said that i am committed to trying to make sure that we use what we have better, that we monitor carefully what is happening and that we use the political and economic instruments at our disposal to keep this at the heart of our agenda for the future, and i am very grateful for all the contributions. to those whose comments and questions i have not answered: it is not lack of will, i will consider them very carefully, and all of this will feed into the debate that we will have at the foreign affairs council at the end of january.

the kidnapping and subsequent murder of antoine de lecour and vincent delory in niger is a painful reminder of the need to implement a strategy to promote security, stability and good governance in the sahel region. the epp group has been a long-standing supporter of such a strategy and i would like to welcome, in this context, the announcement by the european commission that it will present, by the end of this month, a strategy combining security and development aspects. i believe that we really need to look at the question of security in the sahel in all its dimensions, because if terrorism has succeeded in establishing itself in this region, it is also because it has found there political conditions, first and foremost social, and of course, economic conditions. it's about very permeable borders, the absence of effective government control. all of this has obviously allowed the proliferation of illicit trafficking and, in addition, there are development deficiencies. for the security of the sahel and, by implication, of european citizens, i believe that two elements are very useful. first, a strategy for the sahel-saharan region, aimed at restoring the authority of the states in the area over the abandoned territories and, of course, the construction of a state governed by the rule of law. and secondly, i think we need to start joint socio-economic development programmes in border areas to create job opportunities for the local people.
the deterioration of security in the sahel region is no longer a regional problem; unfortunately, it has become a european union problem, with the intensification of attacks on european citizens. the sahel is facing, first and foremost, the ever-increasing terrorist threat, whose victims are primarily europeans, who are being kidnapped and killed with alarming frequency. it is also a transit area for drugs and arms trafficking, as well as a corridor for illegal migration to europe. i believe that there is a need to strengthen concrete cooperation with the north african authorities in order to improve the involvement of the armed forces and security forces in the region in the fight against terrorism. we also have a number of tools at our disposal politically to stimulate regional cooperation to counter this threat. i hope that the european union's technical assistance efforts will be more focused on supporting the development process, because we cannot ignore the fact that terrorist groups find fertile ground in the sahel, particularly because of the poverty of the population and the fragility of state authority. i believe that increased and properly targeted development aid can play a key role in improving the situation in the area.

competition policy is a key element in ensuring the competitiveness of the european economy, and state aid control is an integral part of it. at the same time, in the context of the crisis, the european commission had to approve the granting of state aid, in particular to the banking sector, but also to other sectors that were in difficulty. member states have thus provided substantial amounts in the form of guarantee schemes, recapitalisation schemes and other forms of liquidity financing to banks in order to provide them with a source of funding and a guarantee against risks. the european commission must, however, monitor the sector closely and present plans for the restructuring and regulation of financial institutions to ensure that they do not continue to engage in risky behaviour that endangers the financial stability of the european union. otherwise, the state aid only contributes to perpetuating the financial difficulties in the european union.

rapporteur. − madam president, exactly three years ago the european parliament endorsed the black sea synergy. this was the first step towards a coherent policy in one of the most sensitive areas in europe, and it was a step in the right direction because the black sea is now widely analysed – and feared – as a converging space of political, strategic and security hopes, strengths and ambitions. today our policy in the area can be further developed. this house can play a crucial role in upgrading eu policies to a fully-fledged eu strategy. this is actually the main idea in the report i initiated with the support of my colleagues from the foreign affairs committee and parliament as a whole. but why a new report on the black sea and why an eu strategy for the black sea? some people would say that the black sea is a small sea. indeed it is, but if we exchange this map for a strategy map, the black sea becomes huge. there is also another factor: the black sea is getting blacker and blacker. since the accession of bulgaria and romania, the black sea is now partially an internal eu sea. however, developments in the region are often unpredictable: tensions accumulate and misunderstandings abound. a summary analysis of the black sea region leads to the conclusion that the negative challenges in this area persist or are, indeed, gaining in intensity. the georgia-russia war of 2008, the unsolved and so-called ‘frozen’ conflicts, and the worrying deterioration of democratic rule in ukraine and russia are all very serious developments and vivid examples of the security risks in the area. if we examine the current results of eu involvement in the region, they seem at least mixed. the eu policy approach towards the black sea lacks mechanisms for monitoring, evaluation and follow-up. the black sea region is not visible enough in debates in brussels, and eu funding for the region is fragmented and complicated. while building upon the merits of the black sea synergy which we adopted three years ago, a new eu strategy for the black sea should put in place a stronger policy and concrete tools. let me mention just two of the recommendations in the report. the first concerns adequate resources: if the eu wants to play a key role in the black sea region, it needs to devote adequate resources, both financial and human. the creation of a separate budget line in the eu budget is vital. the second recommendation is for the elaboration of an eu action plan with clear objectives and tasks, including regular ministerial-level meetings of the relevant countries. the eu strategy for the black sea should not underestimate, or overestimate, any state in the area. the principles of inclusiveness and regional ownership should be reflected in an important role for turkey and russia, but also for all the regional partners, in the success of regional cooperation. to conclude, i should like to thank all my colleagues for their very positive contributions to the final version of this report. i think we all agree that this house expects the commission and the council to turn this report into reality. the strategic and beneficial involvement of the eu in the black sea region should become a fact.
reporting for the opinion of the committee on industry, research and energy. − the itre commission supports the full integration of energy markets and the regulatory framework, based on eu legislation, and encourages the participation of the states of the wider black sea region in the energy charter treaty, as well as eu, eib and ebrd assistance in upgrading the energy infrastructure in the region. we underline the european added value and the importance of the southern gas corridor for improving the security of supply of the european union. projects such as nabucco, a priority for the european union, alongside the trans adriatic pipeline, the pan-european oil pipeline, the turkey-greece-italy interconnection and the azerbaijan-georgia-romania interconnection, highlight both the importance of the eu's commitments in the black sea region and the further need to step up cooperation between the countries in the region. we stress the importance of creating a regional research and education network in the wider black sea region and connecting it to geant and invite the commission to continue to support research projects in the region. i would like to conclude, madam president, by asking the commission to develop a european union strategy for the region, accompanied by an action plan, and we stress the need to link this strategy to the european union strategy for the danube region.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on regional development. − madam president, commissioner, the importance of the black sea region for the eu from the transport, energy, stability, security and environmental point of view is evident. it is for this reason that the eu strategy for this region will certainly have a very positive impact on the area and on the eu as a whole. the committee on regional development believes this strategy can bring growth and sustainable development for the region. but also it is of the opinion that for full effectiveness it is necessary to involve all the states of the region, no matter whether they are member states or not. this strategy needs actions to be coordinated – but how could this coordination exist without the proper involvement of all countries? coordination is certainly needed with the danube strategy, which is soon supposed to become a major priority of the hungarian presidency. the use of an integrated approach and cross-border cooperation between the regions should be promoted in all fields of the strategy but in particular those of transport, energy and the environment.
on behalf of the s&d group. – madam president, the black sea is a gate to and from europe, and therefore it should be addressed as such. it is not a far distant place of little relevance which occasionally comes to our attention. the truth is that the area has already put – and will continue to put – items on our agenda, be it through the interruption of gas transit as in 2006 and 2008, or the georgian war in 2008. however, in spite of the evidence and its recognised importance, the black sea area still does not enjoy the attention it deserves from the eu – an eu which was, in a way, compelled to address these problems once bulgaria and romania had become members in 2007. the black sea synergy, elaborated not long after the admission of those two countries, appears to have been, in retrospect, a hastily put together document designed to cover a ‘blank spot’ or ‘black hole’ – depending on your preference – which the eu had to deal with almost overnight. the fact that nothing of importance has happened since the first review of the initiative in 2008 – and we are not very far advanced in its implementation as mentioned in the report – is indicative of that. to my mind, there are two main reasons for this. first, there is an apparent disinterest and unwillingness on the part of eu members to address the area decisively. moreover, now that money is short, there is even less willingness to do so than before. secondly, the initial assumption on which the synergy was based, namely that the area should become a coherent and cooperative region in order to qualify for eu attention and material support, has ignored the simple truth that just 20 years ago the area looked completely different. to expect an area so complex and different to become coherent and get an individual identity in such a short time is either unrealistic or – i hate to say – ill-intended. perhaps, in the context of a revisiting of the eastern partnership, things would improve.
madam president, i should like to start by congratulating mr ungureanu on his initiative in carrying out the report on the black sea. i also welcome the endorsement of several of the previous speakers, my distinguished colleagues, who have committed themselves to promoting a new european vision for the black sea region. the black sea has indeed become a partially internal sea of the european union. its geostrategic importance can hardly be overstated, considering the regional stability, the democratisation processes, and the related energy security, economic and commercial issues. i strongly believe that we, the eu, should benefit from the potential of the black sea region and not others. to achieve this goal, the european union has to rely more on its member states belonging to the region, has to give up any anchorage in the past and has to show more dynamism, leadership and vision. without touching on the issues related to the enlargement process, i would like to address a message to all the black sea sceptics. any slowdown in the eu integration process of the region will have a throwback effect on the democratic evolution of the area. the risk is medium and long-term instability, whose implications would be hard to evaluate, and even harder to manage, for the european union. in conclusion, the eu needs its internal black sea and we need an integrated strategy for this region. the black sea strategy should be drafted by the commission, relying on the recommendations reached by our rapporteur. today this house should offer its wholehearted support for the strategy.
madam president, since 2007 we have acknowledged the importance of the black sea region, yet the impact of our approach has been modest to say the least: no concrete projects, no concrete results. we need a realistic and financially sound action plan with clear objectives, priority actions and benchmarks, and a better division of tasks and coordination with the eastern partnership and the danube strategy. we need to launch the energy and transport partnership alongside the environment partnership. only through such a project-based approach, focused on small-scale specific projects, can we overcome the issue of the very diverse and complex interests in the region. we need to get past our fragmented approach in terms of finance as well. so far, we have had various financial instruments and little visibility. that is why we should make the black sea joint operational programme our central instrument for implementing the black sea strategy, using it as seed money to attract institutions ready to invest in the region and hence promote cooperation.
the black sea region is of strategic importance to the european union. however, we note the lack of a structured approach to this region. no action plan has been drawn up for the black sea synergy and funding is provided through a number of uncoordinated instruments. it is therefore imperative to create a union strategy for the black sea, with the same priority as the other regional strategies of the european union and focused on three main lines: economic, social and human development; energy, transport and environment, and security and good governance. some key projects for the european economy, such as the nabucco pipeline, which would allow for greater energy independence, or the development of ports on the black sea, need to be boosted immediately and this can only be achieved under the aegis of a common strategy.
first of all, i would like to congratulate rapporteur ungureanu on the excellent work he has done on this report of great importance, both geopolitically and economically. the region has significant energy production and supply potential and needs to be given more attention, in particular to ensure the union's energy security. given that the eu's efforts have not been sufficiently well-defined and the black sea synergy has not reached its full potential, i express my hope that the european external action service will have the necessary human and material resources to complete the implementation of the three partnerships: environment, transport and energy. i believe that the european union must not neglect this region, but on the contrary, must make its presence felt through consistent and long-term actions that allow the development opportunities to be exploited.
the black sea is important to the european union for its strategic position, but also for the economic opportunities it offers and the conditions for stronger regional development. the strategy for this area is beneficial in contributing to the diversification of economic activities between the coastal states, the intensification of cooperation in education and research, and the intensification of cooperation in the region, for an important protection of natural resources. i believe that the european union should encourage the countries of the black sea area to make appropriate use of natural environmental resources, to develop the area sustainably and to improve the quality of life in the area, and to build local and regional partnerships.

in writing. confusing objectives and overlapping forms of cooperation risk draining the eu's black sea strategy of its substance. things tend not to improve because of the diversity of the status of the countries involved in relation to the european union, the often divergent interests of the actors in this cooperation and because of a lack of vision, also present in the ungureanu report. if we want to speed up the resolution of the frozen conflicts in the region, we have to start from the fact that this has been long delayed by the competition between the sponsors of the various plans, and things have been training for more than 15 years. and this competition betrays their divergent interests, most often linked, explicitly or implicitly, to control of the energy transport routes in the area. in my view, things will only become clear once it is very clear what will happen with turkey's accession to the eu and what status russia will have in relation to the union. only this clarification will lead to the resolution of frozen conflicts and the long-term stabilization of the area.

in writing. − one of the principles of the treaty on european union is that member states must adopt an economic policy in accordance with the principles of an open market economy based on fair competition. competition policy aims to create real competition in the common market by measures relating to market structures and the behaviour of market players. free competition encourages innovation, reduces production costs, increases economic efficiency and, as a result, raises the level of competitiveness of the european economy. the report covers both antitrust and state aid control policies. it also includes rules and procedures to combat anti-competitive behaviour by companies and to prevent governments from granting state aid that distorts competition in the internal market. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that competition policy is a key instrument for the european union to have a dynamic, efficient and innovative internal market, to be globally competitive and also to overcome the financial crisis. when competition policy is effectively applied, consumers benefit the most.
in writing. − the competition policy report is an important document, which underlines that in times of crisis it is essential to ensure financial stability, to restore credit flows, but above all to ensure that all conditions and checks and controls are in place for markets to function properly. on the other hand, under such circumstances, the competition rules must be applied flexibly, where necessary, without compromising the principles underlying policies in this field. let us not forget that amidst the crisis there have been many calls for the introduction of protectionist policies, which would only deepen and prolong the crisis. competition policy is a key instrument for the eu to have a dynamic, efficient and innovative internal market that is globally competitive; the report's observations and recommendations on sectoral competition policies and on the purpose and destination of state aid are therefore welcome.
in writing. − 2009 was a difficult year for the european union and beyond, marked by a particularly severe financial and economic crisis. the negative effects were felt on the economy and the business environment as well as on decision-makers. while policymakers tried to devise policies that would minimise the impact of the crisis on the real economy, the european commission, together with the member states and central banks, worked hard to stabilise the financial system. this year's report pays particular attention to these issues and welcomes the commission's rapid response and successful use of competition policy measures. i voted in favour of this report because i believe that the european union needs a sound competition policy, based on the principle of open markets and fair competition in all sectors, which will create a successful internal market and foster the creation of sustainable and knowledge-based jobs.

in writing. − the report is important also in that it refers to the importance of the black sea as a natural resource and to the environmental situation in this region; it should not be overlooked that there has been an unprecedented increase in fish mortality in the black sea in recent times. the main pollutants affecting marine biodiversity are the dnieper, don, dniester and danube rivers (which each year dump 60,000 tonnes of phosphorus and 340 tonnes of inorganic nitrogen into the black sea). other factors that contribute to the degradation of the black sea are overfishing and waste. one group of experts estimates that in about 30 years, underwater life will disappear completely from the black sea because of hydrogen sulfide. i believe that these issues should be placed as high on the european agenda as possible.
in writing. − the strategic importance of the black sea in terms of energy, trade and transport can sometimes mean that environmental concerns are sidelined. in its 2007 communication on the black sea synergy, the commission stated that ‘community accession to the convention on the protection of the black sea against pollution is a priority’. in 2008, the commission confirmed that it was ‘examining the conditions for european community accession’. the report we voted on today reaffirms the importance of this convention, and i would like to reiterate the need for the commission to continue towards full eu accession to it. we must work with other partners under this framework to ensure full implementation of the environmental protection measures which the region desperately needs.

shouldn't we be looking to the future? american historian george santayana wrote in 1905, "those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it". during and in the shadow of world war ii, 220 000 roma and sinti were killed, according to the most conservative estimates, simply because they belonged to these two groups - or, as their persecutors put it, to a race. hungarian, czech, romanian, french, german, polish, serbian and who knows what other nationalities. men, women, old people and children. lots and lots of kids. if they were alive today, many of them would be eu citizens. the memories are unanimous about the fact that in the auschwitz-birkenau camp, the families, unlike the jewish prisoners, were allowed to stay together. as one hungarian holocaust survivor put it, "now even the ss knew that gypsy families could not be broken up". they were able to stay together until the night of august 2nd to 3rd, 1944, when the last of the camp's 30,000 inmates were murdered in the midst of the burning of their barracks. the union was reborn from this abyss, the pit and the hell of the purge, after the second world war. the dream of the founding fathers was that the peoples of europe would together deny all that led to such a final denial of human life, to auschwitz and birkenau. the european peoples together, including today's 10 to 12 million roma population in europe. but that's still the past, you might say. where's the future in that?
