mr president, investing in energy infrastructure is to me the starting point in fulfilling our policy goals, ensuring that our citizens and businesses have access to secure and affordable energy in a functioning internal market and achieving the commission’s ambitious energy infrastructure package, which i see as a positive step. however, we should be pragmatic as well as ambitious. instead of pouring buckets of euros into grand projects, we should focus on identifying and financing smaller, cost-efficient and pragmatic projects that can make a significant difference, such as better interconnections. i think we should consider eu project bonds as a solution to encourage needed investment in infrastructure. but, overall, this crisis forces us to adopt a reasonable, open and integrated approach to our energy policy: first, by taking into consideration all components of the energy mix without considering them – or at least some of them – morally unacceptable, and secondly, with an integrated road map, reconciling our sometimes contradictory climate, supply security and competitiveness targets.
the energy summit can re-direct the union on the path to economic growth. the ambition to become the world's most sustainable economy requires a new energy vision for europe. a coherent, community-based approach is needed, both for production and for efficiency. production is about sourcing, transportation, distribution. there are new sources of energy in the black sea and the caspian sea that can be exploited for long periods. new transport routes can be created from this area. the southern corridor and especially nabucco is extremely important in this regard. the danube strategy can also contribute to the development of new gas or oil supply routes. we cannot discuss a common policy without a common energy grid. interconnecting national networks is the first step towards a single internal market for energy. it needs energy efficiency. steps have been taken in this direction, but the union must put the action plan in this area into practice in the coming years. energy efficiency will have a huge impact on economic growth, ways to reduce co2 emissions, and job creation in it, construction and services. as regards the situation in north africa, we must ensure that the proposals for action which the council will make will ensure a peaceful transition in that area and ensure that the new structures come to power in a democratic way.

in writing. the european instrument for democracy and human rights is one of the only eu external policy instruments that still maintains a rigid system of allocation of funds, in that it does not provide for the possibility of exempting from the principle of ineligibility expenditure on taxes, duties and other duties financed by the eu. in the context of a deterioration in the protection of human rights worldwide, i believe it is absolutely necessary for the european union to reassert its role as a world leader in democracy and fundamental rights. in this respect, the flexibility of the european financing instrument is more than necessary to allow the union and the beneficiaries of european financial assistance to have a certain degree of flexibility in the management of the projects they undertake. on the other hand, this flexibility in the allocation of european funds should be closely monitored so that abuses do not occur. in addition to the fact that the approval of the financing of costs related to taxes, duties and other charges must remain an exception and be made on a case-by-case basis, the european parliament must have a right of oversight over the activities carried out by the commission and the strategic documents adopted by it.
in writing. waste electrical and electronic equipment (weee) is the fastest growing waste stream in the eu. proper weee management helps to reuse valuable resources, with major effects on the environment, public health and the creation of green jobs. according to the commission's impact assessment, approximately 24 kg of weee per capita per year is currently generated in the eu, of which only 65% is collected. recycling weee will contribute to the creation of 5-7 times more jobs than incineration and 10 times more than in landfilling. the revision of the directive has allowed for new targets for the collection, recycling and reuse of weee (a recycling target of 50-75% - depending on the category, up from 10 to 6 - and a new reuse target of 5%), as well as tougher measures to prevent the export of electronic waste to developing countries. the responsibilities of producers, consumers and local authorities are more clearly defined to ensure an environmentally friendly treatment. electronic goods manufacturers will have to ensure that waste treatment is funded, with a positive impact by adhering to ecodesign rules, creating products that are easy to repair and recycle.
in writing. the proposal for a directive on waste electrical and electronic equipment, as sent to the european parliament by the commission, is unclear and therefore member states may interpret the types of equipment covered by this directive differently. in addition, the commission will have to develop a common methodology to determine the amount of waste generated in each member state, but this amount of waste generated depends on the specificities of the consumer market, the different life cycle of products and the habits of the population in that member state. the commission notes that the average annual amount of waste generated by the two companies is higher than the average annual amount of waste generated by the two companies. the added value of this directive is its potential health and environmental benefits. proper management of electronic waste could contribute to up to 50-75% recycling and 5% reuse. to achieve this, producers of electronic goods, but also consumers, need to be held accountable. producers will have to finance the treatment of waste, and consumers will have to dispose of e-waste legally at treatment centres.

the fitness check - which we introduced with the industrial policy document, which also looks at the effects on competitiveness and on the legislation in force, will also help small and mediumsized enterprises. i can only thank mr rübig and be pleased that parliament has invited and supported us to commit ourselves to increasing the funding for the next cip ii. in conclusion, i can only assure you of my commitment, because i agree with everything that has been said. as i have always said on all occasions when i have had the opportunity to speak on the subject of policy for small and mediumsized enterprises, i confirm that my priority will be to ensure that bureaucratic barriers, access to credit and a policy of support for small and mediumsized enterprises will be the main feature of the commissioner for industry and entrepreneurship's work in the coming years, that is, until the end of his term. the support of the european parliament is also of fundamental importance to me because, as i said at the beginning of my reply, there is a perfect identity of views between you and me.

with the accessions of 2004 and 2007, it has become legitimate to speak of the danube region as an area of the european union. as a result, following the request of the european council in june 2009, the commission has developed the strategy for the danube region: i would like to congratulate the document on its focus on 11 key areas which will lead, if properly implemented, to sustainable development, job creation and security in the area. i believe that one of the conditions for the success of this strategy is to overcome the difficulties between the different regions through intensive financial and institutional cooperation and better access to existing funds at regional level. last but not least, one factor that may play a major role in its success is energy. fragmentation of energy markets leads to high costs and lack of real competition. i therefore advocate diversifying supply through genuine interconnections and regional markets, which can ensure greater energy security.
the european danube strategy, modelled on the baltic sea strategy, is a means of coordinating eu policies in a number of areas. the strategy will have to respond to the challenges facing the countries in the area: economic and social disparities between the different regions of the danube countries, the intensification of shipping traffic, climate change, cultural diversity, environmental problems and biodiversity. in this respect, i believe that the european danube strategy will be a platform for constant dialogue between the member states and non-member states of the european union and an instrument for achieving long-term benefits at national, regional and local levels. we want a real strategy, based on new technologies, innovation and investment, a strategy which, once implemented, will ultimately lead to an improvement in the quality of life for all european citizens in the danube region.

in writing. the danube has long been a natural border between states and regions, but also an untapped energy and transport opportunity. the danube strategy starts from the principle of reducing these internal barriers, to their elimination in order to improve cooperation between the riverine countries. the danube river basin is the backbone of a sustainable macro-regional construction. the european strategy in this area targets european communities, regions and states, harmonising their needs for economic, social and cultural development while respecting the environmental norms of the danube's natural habitat. the uniform development of this macro-region will contribute to reducing the gaps between regions and facilitate the achievement of the european objective of territorial cohesion. the strategy will provide a platform for strengthening partnerships between authorities at different levels, but also between authorities, the private sector and civil society. without the concrete training of all those mentioned, the realisation of such a complex and comprehensive structure as the danube strategy will remain only a wish. the development of a regional energy market is another area of interest for the danube countries. strategic interconnections between neighbouring states will have a positive impact on energy security and environmental protection, taking into account the sustainable energy potential of the danube macro-region.
member of the commission. − mr president, clearly there is a general appreciation of the progress that has been made in the application of stem cells for therapeutic purposes. we agree that this needs to be encouraged. the issues as raised by the honourable members are firstly on information and secondly on storage. as far as information is concerned, it is important – as we all agree – to provide accurate and objective information to parents and to the general public about the advantages and limitations of the use of stem cells, including cord blood stem cells. providing such information is the competence of the member states, which sometimes vary in opinion and policy regarding the advantages and limitations, as well as the uses, of stem cells. many member states already have in place information campaigns and other information activities. the commission encourages member states to take such actions. as to storage, we know that private firms already offer parents the service of storing cord blood cells. however, several member states have established public cord blood banks based on altruistic and voluntary cord blood donation. eu law on tissues and cells regulates all tissue establishments, whether public or private. it specifies principles of voluntary and unpaid donation, anonymity, altruism of the donor and solidarity between donor and recipient. in 2004, the european group on ethics recommended public storage of cord blood banks to ensure solidarity access to all patients in need.
in writing. the global market for umbilical cord stem cells was worth approximately eur 3.34 billion in 2010. future projections, based on an annual increase of around 27% over the next period, show that it will reach eur 11 billion by 2015. with stem cells seemingly the new 'el dorado' of health research, many researchers are rushing to tackle this niche without ensuring that they meet all the quality and safety standards required for these procedures. i believe that the commission needs to step up its efforts to inform patients and healthcare professionals about the benefits of cord blood stem cell collection, and to make a special effort to ensure that the commission's minimum standards of quality and safety for the donation, procurement, testing, processing, preservation, storage and distribution of human cells and tissues are and will be respected in all member states.
in december 2010, the unemployment rate in the eu27 stood at 9.6%, with 23 million unemployed. compared with last year, the unemployment rate increased in two thirds of the member states. young people and women are the most affected by the economic crisis. for women, the unemployment rate in the eu-27 rose to 9.6% and for young people to 21%. in some countries, such as spain, slovenia, and lithuania, it was as high as 35 percent. also, only 50% of people over 60 are still in the workforce. the main concern of european citizens remains work. i call on the commission and the member states to take the necessary measures to make social europe a reality. european citizens seek decent work, with a wage from which they can live decently, and access to good quality social and health services. i ask the commission and the member states to give priority to allocating financial resources to measures that can create jobs, such as industrial development, in the european union.
i salute the civil movements of the tunisians and egyptians who have succeeded in overthrowing two dictatorial regimes that have been entrenched for several decades. the concern for the future of the arab region, on whose stability the global balance depends, must be matched by a greater concern for the welfare of citizens, both in europe and outside the european union. since the beginning of the economic crisis, the priority has been to save the financial and banking system and to ensure the balance of the state budget. but the burden of the recession is causing unpredictable effects with major geopolitical impact. in tunisia and egypt, rising food prices and unemployment have deepened the exasperation with dictatorial regimes. the lack of perspective and the increasingly oppressive present also influence the mood of citizens in some member states, especially in the east and south of the european union. i think it's time to pay more attention to people's living standards, otherwise we risk seeing unexpected manifestations of discontent from a population that is constantly being asked to make sacrifices.
this regulation constitutes a step forward in the progressive achievement of the co2 emission reduction targets for european light commercial vehicles. this will be achieved by creating incentive mechanisms for vehicle efficiency and imposing penalties on manufacturers who do not meet these targets. i do not think, however, that the new co2 legislation should endanger either the car manufacturers or the car buyer. the new rules should take into account the concerns of smes and european car manufacturers who are demanding that the phasing in of pollution limits start after 2015, as the vehicles to be sold in 2014 are already in the development and production stages. 147 grams is an acceptable compromise compared to the figures that have been circulated. however, the commission must closely monitor the relationship between the car industry and users in order to assess the effect of this measure on prices and, by implication, on the activity of small businesses.
i appreciate the work done by the rapporteur, mr callanan, and by mr groote in bringing this report to fruition. this regulation will force car manufacturers to develop new green technologies and, although it seems a new burden for them, it may lead to increased competitiveness of the automotive industry in the world market. at the same time, it will contribute to the fulfilment of the co2 reduction commitments under the european union strategy. the compromise amendments agreed give manufacturers enough time to prepare for the implementation of new technologies and the commission to prepare an effective mechanism for the prosecution of infringements in this area.

in writing. – the agreement which has been reached with council is the result of tough negotiations in the face of intense lobbying from industry. throughout the whole process, we have resisted heavy pressure from manufacturers to weaken the regulation, and in particular to reduce the ambition of the long-term co2 reduction targets. it was a difficult dilemma, as many of us have car industries which are already struggling because of the economic context. but we knew from our experience with the passenger cars regulation that the car industry has made enormous progress in terms of innovation and developing cleaner technology because the legislative framework encouraged them in the right direction. we wanted to repeat this success with legislation for vans – not just for environmental reasons, but because greater fuel efficiency will ultimately bring costs down for many businesses. we have a compromise text which, although not as ambitious as we would have liked, will lead to a significant reduction in co2 emissions from vans and contribute to the eu’s emission reduction ambitions for 2020 and beyond. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and shadows on their successful negotiations with the council.
in writing. the regulation voted today is a very important success, being the first time that the rights of passengers on buses and coaches will be protected by law. after two years of difficult negotiations, the european parliament and the member states have agreed on the key points that strengthen passenger rights on this transport route. these include compensation for delayed or cancelled travel, compensation for lost or damaged luggage, and liability of companies and assistance in the event of accidents. non-discrimination and assistance to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, and the right of travellers to be informed before and after a journey have been introduced in the regulation as fundamental rights that will apply regardless of the distance travelled. the regulation does not impose new technical requirements but requires carriers to assume responsibility for their passengers. we have also taken into account the current economic situation and its effect on the companies concerned by this regulation, by providing for a derogation period of 4 years, renewable once. i believe that, once it enters into force in 2013, this regulation will contribute to achieving the objective of harmonising and strengthening passenger rights at european level, irrespective of the means of transport chosen.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, at the request of baroness ashton, the hungarian presidency of the council is representing the high representative and vice-president of the commission during this debate. baroness ashton, as you may know, is travelling in northern africa and in the middle east this week. i wish to thank you for raising the issue of the situation of human rights and the rule of law in russia. despite some very positive signals from president medvedev last year, the actual human rights situation in russia and, in particular, in the northern caucasus region, remains deeply preoccupying. violence, harassment and intimidation against activists, lawyers and independent journalists are of great concern to us. the number of cases to support this statement is unacceptably high. the brutal attacks on russian journalists oleg kashin and anatoly adamchuk and environmental activist konstantin fetisov are among the latest reminders of the climate of insecurity and intimidation that journalists, activists and human rights defenders in russia face in their day-to-day work. despite assurances at the highest levels, the perpetrators are rarely brought to justice and sentenced. accountability for violence and intimidation against human rights defenders – let me mention the cases of mrs estemirova, mrs politkovskaya, mrs barburova and mr markelov among a great number of others – remains an important test for the independence and efficiency of russia’s judiciary. as long as the crimes remain unsolved, a climate of impunity will continue to prevail. there are, however, also positive developments. i should mention here the moscow city council’s decision to authorise peaceful and regular demonstrations – which were forbidden until last year – such as those in support of article 31 or the day of press rallies. we have welcomed this decision. at the same time, we continue to receive reports about arbitrary arrests of peaceful demonstrators, including opposition leaders, at these very same authorised demonstrations, as well as others across the country. this is a matter of serious concern to us. freedom of speech and freedom of assembly and association are preconditions for the development of modern societies. all of these freedoms are enshrined in the constitution of the russian federation. they also form part of the commitments that russia has entered into as a member of the united nations, the osce and the council of europe. the eu urges russia to uphold its commitments and guarantee this right to citizens. president medvedev has asked his presidential human rights council to examine the khodorkovsky, lebedev and magnitsky cases. we very much welcome this decision. the eu has made no secret of its serious concerns with the way these cases have been handled. president medvedev has often spoken out against what he has termed the legal nihilism prevailing in russia. the eu stands ready to support russia’s efforts to overcome this, starting with the reform of its judicial system. convinced that real modernisation needs established respect for the rule of law and its equal and fair application, we have put the rule of law at the core of our partnership for modernisation. in this context, concrete activities have already been prepared – for example the setting up of an appeal system for civil and criminal court cases in russia – in close cooperation with the president’s administration and the council of europe. we are ready to work with russia on this, as well as on new projects on corruption and the hague conventions. the situation in the northern caucasus is particularly worrying and needs urgent action. we welcome the new strategy for economic and social development and the efforts by deputy prime minister khloponin, but much more needs to be done to provide a lasting response to the barbaric acts of terrorism against civilians. the continuing immunity and impunity of security forces operating in chechnya is fuelling grievances and terror in the region and is a source of deep preoccupation for us. we pay tribute to all those who have lost their lives and to those who have fallen victim to aggression because of their professions or beliefs, as well as the courageous ones who cannot be deterred from their civil engagement in such a precarious environment. overall, the current report has not been a very positive one. however, there are positive signs in the situation of human rights in russia. these are often offset by backward developments and overall have not been enough to achieve real improvements, but we must not be discouraged. the significant body of european court of human rights case law provides an important incentive for the development of russian law with regard to respect for human rights. we are engaged in a serious dialogue with russia on human rights. russia accepts this and, of course, also uses it to criticise what it sees as imperfections in the eu. we will continue with that dialogue. there is no alternative.
on behalf of the s&d group. – mr president, the model of power-sharing between the state and the members of society determines the content of political decisions, while the predictability of the decision-making process and the correct enforcement of decisions are guaranteed by the honesty, professionalism and independence of the judiciary. the european union and russia can do business together only if there is compatibility between their power-sharing models, their decision-making mechanisms and their judiciary systems. the achievement of such compatibility is an exercise in partnership and cooperation, in consensus, confidence and interoperability-building, not in advocacy, lecturing and finger-pointing. russia is a full member of the council of europe and a signatory to the european convention on human rights. consequently, it is the council of europe that has competence to look into the functioning of democracy and the rule of law in russia. the european union should therefore rely on the council of europe in order to achieve, together with russia, a common area of freedom, democratic security and justice. moreover, since the european union is itself on the way towards accession to the european convention on human rights, it should use its future status as a party to that convention to accelerate convergence and interoperability with russia in the field of democracy and the rule of law. years ago, when the european parliament had little more power than a militant ngo, its only tools were the rhetoric of naming and shaming. today, after lisbon, we are a powerful political institution. this imposes on us more responsibility, pragmatism and self-restraint. we should not let ourselves be led by emotions. we should not be casual with our values either. we are not allowed to be simultaneously prosecutor and judge. we should not act on the basis of mere allegations, rumours or various interest lobby groups. our credibility, generated by the fairness and maturity of our approach, as well as our firmness and openness, is the best weapon we have in our dialogue with russia at a time when our citizens have instructed us to develop a strategic partnership with russia, not to restart the cold war.

in writing. the international press has covered the case of mikhail khodorkovsky extensively and indeed everything seems to indicate that this case has been politically instrumentalized. recent statements by the press officer of judge danilkin clearly indicate the lack of judicial independence in russia. on the other hand, it is important to stress that this is not an isolated case. on the contrary, ngos operating in russia regularly report that fair trial standards are not respected in russia. moreover, in september 2010, the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe called on the moscow authorities to adopt reforms to ensure the independence of the judiciary and to end the harassment of lawyers. finally, it is important to highlight the critical situation in the north caucasus, a region where impunity reigns and where, worse still, victims are afraid to defend themselves, lest they put themselves in even more danger. it is clear that if the russian authorities are to be credible in their stated intention to respect the rule of law, they must make more efforts than they have so far.
in writing. – the rule of president medvedev and prime minister putin is not compatible with the rule of law. for more than 10 years putin and medvedev tolerated, and possibly protected, an appalling catalogue of abuses and crimes, including stage-managed trials, press control and political murder. the horrendous record of lawlessness in russia is not a question of private delinquency. the real problem is state-sponsored lawlessness. the russian justice system, and indeed the russian state, never dealt with crimes aimed at journalists, human rights campaigners and whistle-blowers in the army or in the judiciary. the lawlessness in russia was regarded for too long as an accident or as a problem beyond state control. eu policy should hold the russian authorities responsible for their collusion with criminal elements. recent developments seem to indicate that the second khodorkhovsky trial was conducted at the behest of high political figures. the extrajudicial record of the russian state is already a tradition. the eu policy should take stock of this deplorable practice. the usual soft eu rhetoric is not appropriate. it should be replaced by a resolute policy, including credible warnings that future cooperation with russia requires an immediate improvement in russian law enforcement.

in writing. − the services directive will in no way lead, as some parties speculate, to deregulation or liberalisation of the services sector. its objective is to ensure access to national markets so that arbitrary obstacles are removed and the rules that remain in force in the member states are proportionate and non-discriminatory. the directive explicitly states that neither labour law nor workers will be affected by these legislative provisions. parliament itself insisted on this, imposing its view on the council. article 16 provides that no member state is prevented from imposing certain requirements in respect of a service activity where this is justified on grounds of public policy, public safety and public health or the protection of the environment. there are delays in the implementation of the directive in some member states, but these are mainly due to different interpretations of the directive. it is therefore important that the scope of the directive is clear and transparent. it is necessary not only to draw a clear line between the services covered by the directive and services of general interest, but also to ensure the protection of services of economic interest by means of a legislative framework to that end.
in writing. − the services directive is a key step towards a true single market for services, which will enable businesses, especially smes, to provide citizens with better services at competitive prices. i supported the rapporteur's view that the establishment of one-stop shops is an essential element for the effective implementation of this directive. this tool can be of great importance for small and medium-sized enterprises. the single window should provide accurate, complete and comprehensive information on formalities, administrative procedures, labour law, tax regimes in force in the member states, in particular as regards vat, etc. in addition, business people should be assisted in carrying out the necessary administrative procedures. i consider that, after the completion of transposition, it is essential to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of the services directive on economic activity, the qualitative and quantitative level of employment, social protection, the achievement of environmental objectives and the quality of services provided to consumers.
in writing. − in the european union, over 70 million europeans travel by bus and coach each year. from now on, as a result of the european parliament's strong position on the rights of people travelling by bus or coach, transport operators will provide information, assistance and compensation throughout the union to respect the rights of passengers. whatever means of transport they use, europeans are now protected at european level. i support this report which regulates overbooking of buses and coaches or departures more than two hours late for distances longer than 250 kilometres and cancellation of trips. i also believe that the policy of non-discrimination towards people with reduced mobility is reflected in a set of basic rights regarding assistance at bus stops and bus stations, including free transport for certain equipment such as wheelchairs. i voted in favour of this report which supports the rights of disabled people and people with reduced mobility, such as non-discriminatory access to transport, the right to compensation for loss or damage to wheelchairs or other mobility equipment.
in writing. − the european parliament voted on tuesday to add the missing link to european passenger rights legislation, which is to be applied in a uniform way from spring 2013. it was a difficult negotiation, but it will cover all national or crossborder road transport services over distances of more than 250 km. standards for road transport needed to be standardised as it is increasingly used by european citizens, being cheaper and more advantageous for short distances not covered by air transport. in the context of european traffic, it is normal that the compensatory rules applied to air transport, long since standardized, have a counterpart in road transport. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament and the council should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. every passenger, whether by air or by road, should know his rights, especially when he is paying for one service and sometimes receiving something else entirely. i hope that not too many states will ask for a temporary exemption from these rules and that they will be applied uniformly from 2013.
in writing. − i welcome the fact that the final text can be considered a very satisfactory and well-balanced compromise, as it manages to guarantee passenger rights without at the same time imposing too restrictive measures on carriers, most of which are small and medium-sized enterprises.
in writing. − today, after two years of difficult negotiations with the member states, the european parliament voted to agree on a regulation that will cover all the rights of passengers using national or crossborder long-distance transport services. i voted in favour of this agreement because it contains 12 fundamental rights, which are very important for improving the quality of transport services. these relate in particular to the right of travellers to be informed before and during their journey, and to the needs of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility. by introducing these rights, we will ensure non-discriminatory access to transport. in addition, this report contains passenger rights which i consider very important, namely mandatory compensation for lost luggage, reimbursement of a certain amount for death or bodily injury, and compensation of up to 50% of the ticket price, in addition to full ticket reimbursement, if an operator cancels a journey and is thus unable to honour his transport contract.
in writing. - i voted for the regulation on the rights of passengers travelling by bus and coach. it sets out rights for passengers travelling by bus and coach comparable to those applicable to all other modes of transport. it applies to all scheduled, national and cross-border services with a scheduled distance of at least 250 km. these rights relate to non-discriminatory access to transport for disabled persons and to compensation in the event of death, personal injury or loss of or damage to baggage. if a journey is cancelled or delayed for more than 120 minutes, passengers will be offered either a re-routing to their final destination at no additional cost or a refund of the ticket price. if the carrier does not offer this option, passengers are entitled to compensation of up to 50% of the ticket price, in addition to reimbursement of the ticket price. if a journey of more than three hours is cancelled or delayed by more than 90 minutes, the operator must provide assistance and hotel accommodation, up to eur 80 per night per passenger, for a maximum of two nights. i ask that passengers be adequately informed of their rights in order to be able to claim infringements.
in writing. − i believe that this draft regulation is based on the premise that reducing the fuel consumption of light commercial vehicles will reduce the overall level of co2 emissions in the transport sector, thus mitigating climate change and thus setting co2 emission limits for new light commercial vehicles in the european union.
in writing. − this proposal is a follow-up to the community strategy to reduce co2 emissions from light commercial vehicles (lcvs), as follows: – from 2020 a long-tem target of 147g co2/km for the average emissions of new lcvs registered in the union, subject to confirmation of its feasibility. by 1 january 2013, after a complete review of them, a proposal will amend it, if appropriate; – the short-term target, fixed to 175g co2/km; a phasing-in period from 1 january 2014 onwards with full compliance of the new fleet from 2017;– specific emission target for alternative fuel vehicles will be incorporated, aimed at promoting further deployment of certain alternative-fuel vehicles in the union market; – for multi-stage vehicles, the specific emissions of co2 of completed vehicles will be allocated to the manufacturer of the base vehicle. the super-credits to manufacturers producing lcvs with emissions of co2 of less than 50g co2/km will be limited with a threshold of 25 000 lcvs per manufacturer. – the penalties: from 2019 onwards settled to €95, being phased in gradually from 1 january 2014 to 2018. helping manufactures to develop green technology for vans will be beneficial both for companies and job creation.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation setting performance standards for new light commercial vehicles, as part of the european commission's integrated approach to reducing co2 emissions from light vehicles. we are thus encouraging vehicle manufacturers to use eco-innovation to ensure the competitiveness of the european automotive industry. the regulation imposes penalties on manufacturers of light commercial vehicles for exceeding the average specific emissions set by this regulation. i would point out that limiting emissions must not be approached only from the point of view of supply, for example how to upgrade light vehicles to be less polluting, but also from the point of view of demand. it is important that new vehicles complying with this regulation are accessible to consumers. the regulation thus allows both incentives for the production of fuel-efficient vehicles and penalties for manufacturers who do not meet the agreed targets. each member state shall be required, as from 1 january 2012, to record annually the information relating to each new light commercial vehicle registered in its territory and to ensure compliance with the provisions of this regulation.
in writing. − i voted for this report because i believe that the enhanced cooperation solution for the creation of the unitary patent is the best solution at the moment and i hope that, along the way, all member states will take part in it, for the benefit of european citizens. the single patent will substantially reduce administrative costs for small and medium-sized enterprises, encourage innovation and facilitate the creation of new jobs at a time when the eu increasingly needs them.
in writing. − the internal market is currently highly fragmented due to the high costs of patent protection in the union and european inventors cannot enjoy all the benefits of the single market. the difficult situation arises when they try to achieve an optimal level of protection throughout the union. this has a negative impact on the union's competitiveness, as innovative activities generate human capital that tends to be more mobile than in other areas. the current less favourable conditions for innovation reduce the attractiveness of the union for creation and innovation for both european and non-european inventors. i voted in favour of this recommendation because strengthening cooperation within a group of member states in the area of unitary patent protection will protect the interests of the union by improving its competitiveness and attractiveness for the rest of the world. the creation of unitary patent protection for a group of member states would also improve the degree of patent protection and eliminate the costs and complexity associated with those territories, which would facilitate scientific and technological progress and the functioning of the internal market.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the decision authorising enhanced cooperation in the area of the creation of unitary patent protection because i consider it necessary to adopt measures for the creation of a unitary community patent. according to a 2011 thomson reuters report, "patented in china", china will surpass japan and the united states in the number of patents. thus, through the programme launched in 2006, china aimed to become an innovation-oriented country and managed to increase the number of patents by 14.1% compared to the us, 33.55% compared to the eu and 15.9% compared to japan. in the eu, the current patent system is fragmented and very costly in terms of translation requirements. the cost of an eu patent validated in 13 countries amounts to eur 20 000, of which approximately eur 14 000 is for translation costs alone. thus, a european patent costs 10 times more than a us patent. i believe that authorising enhanced cooperation for the creation of unitary patents can contribute to the development of a unitary patent attractive to users of the patent system in europe, provide protection for intellectual property throughout europe and eliminate costs and complications in order to stimulate research, development and innovative smes.
in writing. − this report sets maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination for food and feed following a nuclear accident or other radiological emergency. i agree that the european parliament must play a decisive role in situations which directly affect the health of the population. i also believe that in the aftermath of a nuclear accident or radiological emergency, the european commission should have a supervisory role, declaring a state of emergency and adopting lists of basic foodstuffs and feed. member states must maintain an official control system for these products and inform the public of the risks. i voted in favour of this report which guarantees the safety of european citizens' food in the event of nuclear accidents or radiological emergencies.
in writing. − i believe that eu member states are responsible for monitoring compliance with the levels set out in the framework of protection against radioactive contamination in this regulation, in particular by monitoring safety standards for both food and feed, but also by monitoring environmental parameters. i support the idea of a system allowing the eu to set maximum permitted levels of radioactive contamination to ensure a high level of protection of public health following a nuclear accident or other radiological emergency.

member of the commission. − mr president, the green paper on pensions which we published last summer started a much needed debate on the future of pensions in europe. it resulted in more than 100 meetings and conferences with stakeholders and we received almost 1 700 responses. the green paper outlines the key challenges facing the union in this area, and asked fourteen questions about how work at eu level could help the member states in ensuring that pensions are adequate, sustainable and safe, while fully respecting the principle of subsidiarity. the green paper takes a holistic approach, because my fellow commissioners rehn and barnier and i are convinced that adequate, sustainable and safe pensions call for coordinated, joined-up policies spanning our three areas of responsibility. let me briefly restate the commission’s reasoning for publishing the green paper last year. first, we need to overcome the imbalances resulting from the increasing divergence between life expectancy and retirement ages. second, we need to adjust the european framework to reflect the changes that have come about in national pension systems after a decade of pension reforms. third, we must draw lessons from the financial and economic crisis. the crisis has highlighted the need to review financial market exposure and the design of our pension systems in order to improve risk mitigation and enhance the funded pension’s capacity for shock absorption. fourth, we need to fully prepare our pension systems for the acceleration of population ageing. the member states have already engaged in long-standing cooperation to learn from each other’s experiences and exchange good practice in pension reform. there is a consensus on the need for coordination at eu level and for establishing eu rules on cross-border issues. for the last 10 years, coordination at eu level has underpinned member states’ efforts to modernise the pension systems, and many member states have already made good progress in adapting the pension systems to reflect demographic ageing, changes in the labour markets and evolving gender roles. however, most member states have a long way to go and a few others have not even begun with pension reforms. i was pleased to read the report, on which i congratulate the rapporteur, which is highly supportive of the holistic approach we have chosen. in several places it highlights the links between adequacy, sustainability and safety. it also clearly identifies policy areas where the eu can add value. the commission is currently in the final stages of analysing the results of the consultation, including the final opinion of the european parliament. given the urgency of the situation, the commission has already started the preparations for the white paper to be presented in the third quarter of 2011. let me conclude by saying that one of the great successes of europe’s social model is to ensure that old age is not synonymous with poverty. this is a promise on which we have to continue to deliver and help member states to take the right decisions to ensure that pension systems are fit for purpose. the last 12 months have seen a lively debate in the field of pension reforms and this year promises to be equally intense. i very much count on parliament’s support to bring about a real change to create both adequate and sustainable pensions for the future.
rapporteur for the opinion, committee on economic and monetary affairs. - the fact that we are talking about pensions today in the european parliament's plenary confirms their european value. the ageing of the population, the effects of the economic and financial crisis and the late entry of young people into the labour market require common solutions. but pensions remain a national responsibility, and the principle of subsidiarity sets the limits of european intervention. however, if member states better implement existing legislation at european level, we will benefit from a better functioning of the single market and encourage greater mobility of workers. also, for public pension systems to be sustainable, we need to ensure that people have the chance to stay in the workforce until retirement age. the increase in unemployment among member states is a worrying phenomenon, which threatens the principle of solidarity between generations. thus, pension reforms must go hand in hand with the promotion of employment policies. equally, pension reform should not be synonymous with depriving already vulnerable groups of a secure and decent income. states must not abdicate their duty to provide adequate pensions for all citizens. to avoid such abuse at national level, we have put forward the idea of defining an adequate pension at european union level. the requirement that member states guarantee a level of pensions in the first pillar above the poverty line is not, in my view, sufficient. i certainly understand the argument of the diversity of national contexts and the reluctance of states to allow for the involvement of the european union in the very heart of national sovereignty. however, i believe that the european courts must pay greater attention to the living conditions of european citizens. social discontent can have unintended consequences: two recent examples, outside the european union, speak to the tolerability of a population that is constantly sacrificed to the interests of national powers that pay little attention to the needs of citizens.
madam president, i would first like to say that the crisis and demography are combining to make us tackle this problem of pensions in all the member states of the european union. in this work, i would first of all like to welcome a working approach, that of the consultation which commissioner andor told us she had chaired in the preparation of this green paper, but also the work of consultation, openness and compromise which was put in place by ria oomen-ruijten to conduct this report. i would like to stress three points which we must take into account when solving the problem of pension solvency. the first is the inequality that women are now experiencing at retirement age because career inequality leads to poverty at retirement. the second point is that i want to see to it, commissioner, that the old age pension is saved. we are still facing a generation of poor women who have not worked during their working lives and for whom reversal is the only way to have a minimum pension. the third point is the entry of the younger generations into the labour market. they not only have to face the crisis, but also the burden of several generations that they have to bear: that of their children, their parents and their grandparents. finally, this raises the problem of the elderly, on which the time spent at work must be accelerated.
i think we have to be realistic to recognize that the current public pension systems based on the transfer of resources between generations, the so-called pay as you go principle, are no longer economically viable and, not being economically viable, require subsidies from public budgets to survive: the ageing of the population, the increasing mobility of the workforce only deepen the imbalances in these pension systems, and the proposed measures, whether raising the retirement age or increasing contributions, have limits and will be increasingly limited by social resistance to such measures. we will eventually have to recognize that the solution is to move to those pension systems where people during their working lives build up their own pension fund.
i would like to mention that, at the very beginning of this debate, the commissioner spoke of the successes of the european social model. one of them is the achievement of equal opportunities between women and men. i hope this report sends a clear message about mainstreaming gender equality in achieving a fair pension system. so let me emphasize two points. first, the assessment of the impact on society and women's employment of measures to recognise domestic work, including by calculating the financial value of such work for the purpose of calculating pensions. i call on the commission to initiate the procedure for the repeal of article 5 (2) of directive 113/2004, which allows discrimination against women in relation to pension products.

in writing. i believe that the eu needs to build an open single pension system that takes into account demographic trends and the issue of mobility. i'll give the example of my country. annual pension expenditure is the largest category of budget expenditure in romania. the state social security budget has been running annual deficits since 2006, reaching eur 1,5 billion in 2009. according to world bank estimates, by 2050, the pension deficit in gdp under the old system would have reached about 12 percent. therefore, by adopting law no 263/2010, romania has introduced a series of major reforms that will ensure the sustainability of the public pension system in the medium and long term. these include: - discouraging early retirement and invalidity pensions without medical justification; - increase in the number of contributors to the single public pension scheme; - gradual raising of the standard retirement age for men and women to 65 for men by 2015 and 63 for women by 2030.

system; secondly, by introducing market surveillance by national authorities, which must check the declarations of conformity of manufacturers and the certificates of third bodies authorising the affixing of the ce marking on products; thirdly, by obliging member states to strengthen customs controls so that only products which comply with the legislation are allowed to circulate on european and world markets. by providing the instruments for protecting the ce mark which were lacking until recently, the effective implementation of the new regulatory framework strengthens the credibility of the mark and thus the good reputation of the products bearing the mark on the european and, consequently, on the international market. moreover, the reinforced controls on imported products will ensure that there is less abuse of the ce marking also on the world market. furthermore, following an explicit request from the european parliament itself, the commission has successfully launched an today, 1.4 billion people in the world lack access to electricity, 85 percent of them living in rural areas. the millennium development goals to eradicate poverty by 2015 will not be achieved without substantial progress on energy access. achieving this goal by 2015 means that 395 million people will have access to electricity and 1 billion people will have access to sanitary cooking facilities. all of this will require annual investments of about $40 billion between 2010 and 2015, representing 0.6% of global gdp. universal access to electricity is one of the most important goals set by governments in developing countries. barriers to electrification identified include high costs for providing electricity to rural areas and to suburban housing, lack of fiscal or financial incentives, weak capacity to develop and implement electrification projects, and limited electricity generation capacity. rural areas have a particular energy situation. in these areas, not only the energy needed must be secured, but the process of producing it, which also ensures job creation and economic and social development. on 11 february 2011, a world bank report showed that local renewable energy production at low production prices is more economically viable in the long term. this can play an important role in increasing india's energy security, reducing energy imports and reducing the influence of oil price fluctuations. the world bank could therefore be a partner for developing countries. i believe that the world bank should support projects to increase energy efficiency, local production of renewable energy, as well as large-scale electrification and interconnection projects between different countries.

in writing. – the eu 2020 strategy should help europe recover from the crisis and come out stronger, through jobs and smart, sustainable and inclusive growth based on five eu headline targets as regards promoting employment. a strong social protection system, investment in active labour market policies and education and training opportunities for all are essential to reduce unemployment and prevent long term exclusion. the flexicurity is not applicable in member states with low possibilities of strengthening social protection systems due to budget restrictions and macroeconomic imbalances, as in romania, and i consider that reducing labour market segmentation has to be achieved by providing adequate security for workers under all forms of contracts. any labour market reforms must be introduced by reaching a high degree of social consensus through agreements with the social partners at national and eu level. a legislative agenda is essential to eradicate the existing pay gap between women and men by 1% every year in order to achieve the target of 10% reduction by 2020. the eu 2020 strategy should include a target of reducing poverty amongst women in the eu as 17 % of the women are classed as living in poverty, mostly single mothers, immigrants and older women.
in writing. the eu 2020 strategy should be supported by the 2014-2020 financial framework. transport, energy and communications are the backbone of the european economy. investment in these areas will create jobs and ensure economic and social development. the union's industrial policy is a key element of the eu 2020 strategy. the development of industry and job creation within the eu will ensure the union's international competitiveness. in recent decades, the drive for profit of european companies has led to the relocation of industrial production to third countries with low production costs and the loss of jobs in the eu. a strong and well-funded cohesion policy, covering all european regions, must be a key complementary element of the eu 2020 strategy. this horizontal approach is a precondition for the successful achievement of the objectives proposed in the eu 2020 framework and for the achievement of social, economic and territorial cohesion. an example of this is the eu strategy for the danube region, which will contribute to prosperity, economic and social development and security in the region. as the main concern of european citizens remains workplace safety, i believe that the eu 2020 strategy will only succeed if social europe becomes a reality.
i would like to return to some of the points i raised in some of the amendments tabled with my colleague bernd posselt, which have been successfully passed in the committee on foreign affairs. first, i would like to reiterate the hope that the accession negotiations with croatia will be concluded in the first half of 2011, as announced in the programme of the hungarian presidency. from this point of view, it would be a symbolic gesture because it would be 20 years since the declaration of independence from the former yugoslav republic. such an end to the negotiations would also be a very strong signal to the other balkan candidate countries, given that, as we know, the union's attractiveness seems to be declining. finally, i would like to underline the determination of the croatian authorities to fight corruption and organised crime. it's a sign that, as we've seen before, corruption is not inevitable if there's political will.
in writing. − counterfeit medicines are a global threat. representatives of the world health organization (who) warn that counterfeit products do not contain the active ingredients listed in the package insert, but on the contrary, they are based on substances with a high degree of toxicity to the body. i believe that european citizens should be informed at both european and national level about the health risks of ordering products from various uncontrolled websites or from the illegal supply chain, given that the internet is one of the main ways for counterfeit medicines to enter the market in the eu. i support the new legislative proposal because it aims to update the existing regulations and introduce so-called safety features to guarantee the identification, authentication and traceability of medicines from the factory to the consumer, which is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − i voted for this report because the quality and safety of medicines is a growing concern for european citizens. patients must be absolutely sure that the medicines they are taking are indeed the medicines they expect to take. the use of counterfeit medicines can result in treatment failure and can endanger lives. like the rapporteur, i consider that the falsification of medicines is a criminal offence, which deprives patients of the necessary medical treatment and harms their health, sometimes even leading to death. for this reason, the first and foremost objective of the directive should be to protect public health against falsified medicines. the public should also be made more aware of the risks of buying medicines online. we need to guarantee patients that they can recognize sites that are compliant with the law. a directive aimed at combating the counterfeiting of medicines without targeting the internet, the most important means of dissemination, cannot be justified in the eyes of the public.
in writing. − counterfeiting medicines has become a profitable business with minimal risk of prosecution. this is demonstrated by the fact that in 2008 alone, customs authorities announced the seizure of more than 34 million counterfeit medicines in europe. it is true that the eu is not yet in the position of other geographical areas where up to 30% of medicines on the market are counterfeit. but the eu must not allow itself to be in this situation. at present, it is estimated that 1 percent of the medicines sold are counterfeit, but there are warnings that the proportion is increasing. the new safety rules adopted by parliament, the sanctions imposed on manufacturers of counterfeit medicines and the control system between producers and consumers are designed to stop the growth of the black market in medicines in the eu. the introduction of new mandatory safety rules for the trade in medicines, including online sales, is therefore welcome. selling counterfeit medicines is a criminal activity with serious consequences, which can affect a very large number of consumers who often choose the easy way of the internet to order medicines that they would otherwise not have access to in the absence of a medical recommendation.
in writing. − in view of the increasing risks that counterfeit medicines pose to patients, i consider it necessary to introduce urgent interim measures to increase patient safety. those measures should provide that manufacturing authorisation holders who remove or cover visible safety features voluntarily applied by the manufacturer are strictly liable if their actions result in the entry of counterfeit products into the supply chain.
in writing. − counterfeit medicines are a real threat to the whole european pharmaceutical system, because, in addition to the danger to patients who consume such products, the public's confidence in the quality of medicines available in pharmacies is diminished. the number of falsified medical products is skyrocketing in the eu, and they may contain substandard or falsified substances, or they may be missing or in the wrong doses. although the scale of this problem is still relatively small in europe, unlike in other regions, i voted in favour of this report because i believe that there are a number of factors which indicate the need for prompt action at eu level. the new directive will include penalties for manufacturers of counterfeit medicines, enhanced safety rules and a verification system to prevent dangerous medicines from reaching the european market. the european parliament has been successful in adding to the european commission's proposal the regulation of the sale of these products via the internet, which is the main means of introducing counterfeit medicines to the eu market.
in writing. − there is an alarming increase in the eu of medicinal products which are falsified with regard to their identity, history or source. the directive introduces obligatory safety features for all prescriptive medicinal products and a rapid alert system; harmonised safety features to verify authenticity and identify individual packs, providing tampering evidence for medicinal products subject to prescription (possible exclusion of certain products following a risk assessment); no safety features for medicinal products not subject to prescription, unless a risk assessment demonstrates the risk of falsification and consequently a threat to public health; traceability: there will be a unique identifier for the safety features (e.g. a serialisation number) which allows the authenticity of the product and individual packs to be verified throughout the supply chain up to pharmacy level; in addition, member states have to set up systems to prevent suspected medicinal products from reaching patients; internet sales: conditions for the supply of medicinal products to the public are determined by member states; increased transparency as regards wholesale distributors; penalties applicable to infringements of national provisions must be applied.
in writing. − the opportunities for selling falsified medicinal products have increased rapidly in recent years. the ever-increasing risk of these medicines entering the supply chain means there is an urgent need to update the legislation. in particular, regulation of sales on the internet is notoriously difficult and can only be tackled effectively at international level. this issue was not addressed in the commission's proposal, and the work of the envi committee has therefore substantially improved it by adding important safeguards for consumers who purchase medicines online. but the nature of the internet means that we cannot eliminate the risk. consumer awareness of this risk needs to be improved, and so i welcome the inclusion of awareness-raising campaigns for the public which has been agreed as part of the compromise. the commission is in a unique position to coordinate education campaigns for the public and must ensure that the member states fulfil their obligations in this regard.
in writing. - i am impressed by the number of smes in the union, 23 million, and the number of jobs they provide - 100 million. these figures clearly demonstrate that we need to strengthen the financing system for this sector. the european funding system is as diverse as it is complicated. i agree with the initiators of this resolution, the system must be as coherent as possible in the funding period 2014-2020. i support the idea of the initiators to ask the commission to encourage the member states to carry out the necessary reforms. these smes meet in the single market but have different support conditions in their national environments. i also believe that a single window for all eu financial instruments for smes is useful as a solution to balance national support systems with european ones.
in writing. − i believe that the european commission's strategies, acts and concrete action plans for european smes need to be improved and i support the creation of a new european microfinance instrument for employment and better regulation, access to the single market and finance for smes.
in writing. − in the european union, the number of pensioners is increasing due to the increase in life expectancy. pension schemes are the responsibility of the member states, with different rules on retirement age and money spent on social security. the financial crisis has led to an increase in unemployment, poverty and social exclusion, increased budget deficits and problems in the financing of pensions, and has demonstrated the fragility of certain financing systems. the prevalence of temporary work has reduced the level of contributions to pension schemes, damaging their stability. without calling into question the prerogatives of the states and without suggesting that one model would fit all, the european parliament's report and the european commission's green paper call for the maintenance of pension systems adapted to the needs of citizens. i believe that solidarity between states and between generations is an important aspect of the success of community policies. at european level, pension system aspects related to the functioning of the internal market, compliance with the requirements of the stability and growth pact and the 2020 strategy are coordinated. i voted in favour of this report, which supports the efforts of the member states to meet the expectations of citizens for an adequate, viable and secure pension system.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report and i agree with the rapporteur, who speaks clearly and forcefully about the need for solidarity between generations, but also about the major differences between national pension systems in europe. i agree that coordination is needed at union level, and the best arguments are given by the very effects of the crisis, which we hope we have emerged from: the impact of public spending in one member state is easily transmitted to another member state, and pension funds are part of financial markets. i welcome the idea of a flexible labour market for pensioners, given the demographic changes we are experiencing and the obvious trend towards longer careers. i agree that each member state, and the union as a whole, needs to adapt its policies to the concept of active ageing.
in writing. − publicly funded pension schemes in some member states are facing high cost increases, which means increased pressure on solidarity and a heavier burden on the younger generation. 2060 may seem far away, but that doesn't change the predictions: an aging population, a low birth rate, and therefore enormous pressure on budgets. it is clear that each of the member states is directly responsible for setting pension systems, and this prerogative is unquestionable, nor is it suggested that one model would fit all. but the call for adequate, viable and secure pensions is important as europe faces a demographic disaster in a few decades, with the first signs already showing. raising the retirement age is one of the relevant solutions when it comes to the fact that the state will no longer have enough active population to pay pensions to those who have left the labor market. and gradually raising the retirement age is a normal solution under these circumstances, coupled with the fact that life expectancy is much higher than it was 40 years ago.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution for which i was appointed rapporteur by the econ commission. i find the final text of the resolution to be balanced, underlining both the importance of the public pension pillar and the need for a real secondary pillar in all member states. one idea i tried to put forward was the definition of a minimum pension at european level, which would guarantee a secure and decent income for european citizens. unfortunately, it didn't get enough of an echo among my colleagues. i hope, however, that in future the commission will come forward with a proposal of this kind.
in writing. − i welcome the fact that strategy 2020 supports an active and focused labour market policy, which will allow employment growth for older workers, women, members of minority groups and the long-term unemployed. by achieving this, i believe that europe will see an increase in the number of people in the labour force and, by implication, economic growth with positive effects on the viability of pension systems at european level.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because i believe that pension systems across the european union are already facing major sustainability problems, which risk becoming even more serious in the future, and therefore need to be reconsidered. the review by each member state must, however, be made with due regard for the fundamental objective of ensuring a decent income at a reasonable cost for older people after a lifetime of contribution. the reduction of pensions below the subsistence level, which is practised in some member states, is inhumane and must be avoided. the most egregious example of abuse is romania, where the current government has decided that all pensions should be drastically reduced, taxed and taxed for social health insurance. under the guise of subsidiarity, the romanian government is probably trying to create an original pension system by physically disappearing pensioners, depriving them of the minimum financial resources and medical care. i believe that one of the eu's objectives in this area must be to curb the excesses of certain member state governments against pensioners.
in writing. − in november 2009, there were 5.54 million pensioners and 5.65 million taxpayers in the public pension system in romania. ensuring an adequate and sustainable pension for eu citizens now and in the future is a priority for the european union. achieving these objectives in an ageing europe is a major challenge and member states need to prepare for it through pension reforms. member states should strengthen the adequacy of pensions by tackling gender discrimination in the labour market, in particular by reducing pay gaps by at least 10% by 2020. the public pension system must be strengthened at the expense of the private one. we must not privatize the public pension system just to ensure the stability of pension funds for current and future pensioners. although the trend at european level is towards increasing the retirement age, the retirement age should apply flexibly depending on the sector, the severity of working conditions and the number of years worked. active support for job creation is needed and the quality of work needs to be improved to increase the number of people actively contributing to the financing of their future pensions.
in writing. − there are different pension systems in the 27 member states of the european union. but the reversal of the demographic pyramid and the increase in life expectancy imply the need for a european strategy to strengthen pension cohesion and coherence in the european union. i would also like to mention the dysfunctions that arise in the case of labour mobility between different member states. there are cases where pension rights are not transferred adequately between different eu member states. in this respect, we must encourage cooperation between member states. on the other hand, it is our moral duty to ensure that our citizens have the right to a pension that ensures them a decent living.
in writing. − the green paper 'towards adequate, sustainable and secure european pension systems' by ms ria oomen-ruijten makes an important contribution to the debate on the future of european pension systems. i consider it necessary for the member states to draw up provisions on the provision of adequate pensions for their citizens. we encourage member states to establish the most appropriate pension system to guarantee a decent standard of living for all, with special attention to the most vulnerable groups in society. i voted for recital 24, which calls on the member states to encourage the continuation of the professional activity of older people by means of tax exemptions and social security contributions. i also voted for encouraging and facilitating the integration of work and retirement and for implementing disincentives to make it more difficult for older people to be made redundant by the company. i voted against raising the retirement age because i believe that people over a certain age who want and can work should be encouraged to work and not forced to, especially with the unemployment rate in the eu27 at 10% and 20% for young people.

on behalf of the s&d group. – madam president, for years the euro-atlantic players thought that islam could not possibly produce democratic behaviour and institutions. therefore, they opted for either supporting authoritarian regimes or mechanically transferring the western model of democracy to the arab countries. not only did both strategies fail, but they are responsible for the emergence of islamic fundamentalists and the alienation of secular parts of the civil society. the present events in egypt prove that islam need not only be fundamentalist, but that it can also be democratic if we accept that democracy may have a variable geometry, and if we let it grow naturally from its specific soil. at the same time, we must admit that the popular uprising was on one hand the result of the evolution of egyptian elites in the cyber or internet society, and on the other hand the consequence of the existential hardships brought on by the global economic crisis. if the european union does not immediately and consistently address the need to overcome these hardships, the revolution might move towards anarchy; and from there towards another dictatorship. finally, we must not only applaud the fact that no israeli flags were burnt during the recent events in egypt, but also observe that the lack of a long-due solution to the israeli-palestinian conflict is at the origin of the feeling of failure which upset arab society and fuelled its neurosis. therefore, the european union should immediately take the initiative in order to use the transformation in egypt – which today is a mere hope – and turn it into a real opportunity for internal democracy and regional peace. in this context, the trips of the high representative/vice-president to the region, and her readiness to adapt and upgrade the necessary european instruments to cope with the challenges, are good news. her action must be supported by all of us.
18 days of revolt, the resignation of hosni mubarak, the takeover by the military's supreme council, basically the way is open for a transition. our hope is that this transition will be one towards democracy. things are moving, that's for sure, with a speed that, in principle, revolutionary events have. in the last few days, as you know, the constitution has been suspended, the parliament dissolved, the constitutional review commission is proposing amendments in 10 days, legislative and presidential elections are in six months. i believe that the european union must support by all means any gesture which implies a democratic transition. on the other hand, i would like to warn against a certain form of precipitation, because all these construction processes require a certain amount of time. let us also not forget that democratic forces are in critical need of rebuilding and strengthening, lest they contribute to the destabilization of the political landscape.
