in writing. − i voted in favour of the resolution on the proposal to amend directive 2001/112/ec on fruit juices and certain similar products intended for human consumption, as i believe that the implementation of the new provisions will better protect consumers' interests and stimulate the free movement of fruit juices within the eu. the eu fruit juice market accounts for 10% of total consumption of soft drinks and the production of concentrated fruit juice is predominant over the direct juice production (87,6% and 12,4% respectively). the specific provisions and rules on the production, composition and labelling of fruit juices laid down in directive 2001/112/ec need to be adapted to technical progress and take account of the evolution of international standards in this field, in particular the codex standard for fruit juices and nectars (which lays down quality factors and labelling requirements) and the code of good practice of the european fruit juice association. the amendments to the directive aim to align with those standards and reaffirm the distinction between fruit juice and fruit juice obtained from concentrate, simplify the provisions on the restoration of taste and aroma and include tomatoes in the list of fruits and vegetables used for the production of fruit juices.

in writing. − when talking about household laundry detergents, i.e. those used in dishwashers, there must be a balance between the substances used in detergents to ensure their effectiveness and the impact of those substances on the environment. in the case of phosphates and phosphorus compounds, there is a risk of degradation of ecosystems and of algal growth, which needs to be managed. the agreement struck achieves such a balance by limiting the phosphate content of detergents and dishwashers, and in particular by limiting their application over time. it is clear that limiting the phosphate content has the effect of encouraging innovation and the introduction of detergents that are equally efficient but have a lower environmental impact. we must allow time for the development of such substitutes. therefore, i fully support the solution reached for dishwasher detergents, for which the limitation applies from 2017, which leaves enough time for the development of new products, but also for the reporting by the commission, so that we can see if the proposed limit is relevant.

in writing. − phosphorus contributes to the development of life, algae and other plant life, and thus to the eutrophication of water. phosphates are used in detergents to counteract the hardness of water, to allow efficient cleaning and to improve the cleaning performance of detergents. a number of member states already have restrictions on household laundry detergents, and some are introducing restrictions on mav (dishwasher detergents). at eu level, however, legislation is not harmonised, the internal market for detergents is fragmented and difficulties are encountered in the eu's attempts to reach agreements with member states on the reduction of phosphorus in detergents for washing machines and dishwashers in regional water-cleaning initiatives such as the baltic sea action plan, helcom and the danube strategy. the inclusion of mav detergents in the regulation can help to accelerate the campaign against eutrophication, but also to reduce job losses in smes producing phosphate-rich mav detergents and not yet having the knowledge and technology to produce them without phosphates. since there are no statistics on the number of jobs at risk, i ask the commission to draw up a study on this.

in writing. − the current economic crisis has had a major impact on the defence sector. many weapons programs are in danger of being canceled or have even been canceled. the recent nato intervention in libya has exposed many of the limitations of the eu member states' militaries. we are obliged to do more and faster to build a genuine european arms industry. this would eliminate many parallels, avoid waste of resources and allow for better use of production capacities. i think that more attention should be paid to the future needs of the eu countries' armies, drawing on the lessons of recent conflicts and new geo-political data. we are, i think, aware that our nations will not accept an increase in military spending in the context of drastic cuts in budget spending. that's why we need to spend defense money with the utmost care on well-defined programs designed to address the challenges we face. the best level of military spending must be identified, a level that ensures our security in the medium and long term without wasting human and material resources.
in writing. − i voted in favour of this report because defence is a public good that has an impact on the security of all european citizens and all member states must contribute in a spirit of cooperation, shared responsibility and cost efficiency. the financial crisis has led to unprecedented cuts in defence budgets in most member states, which can have negative effects on the eu's ability to maintain peace, prevent conflict and strengthen international security. for this reason, i believe that a strengthened european defence capability will increase the eu's strategic autonomy and make an important contribution to collective security in the context of nato and other partnerships. i also believe that the economic crisis we are facing today can be an opportunity for the integration of eu defence policies, as this can provide the necessary impetus for the creation and implementation of ambitious reforms. i therefore support the call for the development of eu defence policies leading to sound research and technological and industrial cooperation between member states to strengthen the competitiveness and resilience of the defence industry.
in writing. − following the financial crisis, there have been significant cuts in defence budgets in most member states. this may have negative effects on the military capabilities and therefore on the eu's ability to effectively assume its peacekeeping responsibilities. i voted in favour of the report drawn up by krzysztof lisek. an analysis of the possibilities to provide support to member states for the achievement of the objectives of the common security and defence policy in a more cost-effective manner is necessary. the current situation may lead to the loss of certain military capabilities that are vital for the security of european citizens.
in writing. − i voted in favour of the european parliament's report on the impact of the financial crisis on the defence sector in the eu member states, which notes with concern that recent budget cuts represent the continuation of a pattern of underinvestment and underspending in security and defence, which has persisted in the member states for over a decade. promoting a european defence technological and industrial base can create sustainable jobs for european citizens in the eu defence industries. i stress that security research must be retained as an independent component in the next horizon 2020 programme. the area of study of security-related topics should also be broadened to reflect the need for the transfer of innovation and technology between the civil and defence industries. as civil research results often have defence applications, defence research results often benefit society as a whole, as is the case with the internet and gps. we believe that in the long term, greater attention to defence research could be considered in the next framework programmes, in order to stimulate collaborative european research and to help pool disparate national funds.

the reporter. − the european parliament was asked to give its consent to a protocol amending the partnership and cooperation agreement between the european union and uzbekistan so that trade in textiles would benefit from an appropriate legal framework. it is currently lacking, as textiles were a sensitive point in the 1990s negotiations for partnership and cooperation agreements with the countries of the former soviet union. the protocol in question seeks to include textiles in the agreement, so that the legal security of exporters from the european union is guaranteed. beyond this general context, however, there is a serious problem to which the european parliament cannot fail to react: the allegations of the use of child labour in the cotton fields of uzbekistan. this is the main reason why, following the discussions in the commission, i decided to draw up this interim report. uzbekistan ranks fifth in the world in cotton production and third in cotton exports. according to several reports by the initiative group of human rights activists in uzbekistan, conducted in partnership with the international civil rights forum, as well as the uzbek-german human rights forum or the non-governmental organization anti-slavery international, in uzbekistan the political and economic systems are controlled by the state. cotton is produced on private farms, but the harvested cotton must be sold to state-owned firms at a price set by the state. according to the same reports, government agencies are mobilizing children as a cheap source of labor during the cotton harvest. estimates range from 200,000 to 2,000,000 children between the ages of 9 and 15, and the state sets the cotton quotas, and these must be met. schools are obliged to send children to the cotton fields. administrative staff and teachers who refuse to obey risk losing their jobs. families of children who refuse to work are subjected to pressure from the police and the prosecutor's office, who threaten to withhold pensions and social benefits, cut off electricity, gas, and water, and even arrest, detain, and prosecute family members of those who do not comply. many schools, especially those in agricultural areas, are closed from september to november or december. thus, children in these schools miss two to three months of schooling each year. the uzbek government denies the existence of these problems and says that they are related to family farming activities. following constant allegations of forced child labour, the uzbek government was forced to ratify the two ilo conventions on child labour in 2008, after which it approved the national action plan for their implementation. over time, several international organizations such as the un and ilo have expressed concern about the use of forced child labor in uzbekistan. however, the uzbek government does not allow independent international observers to enter the country during the harvest season to verify the application of iom conventions. as rapporteur, i've tried to meet with all the parties involved in this agreement. i regret that it was not possible to have an exchange of views in the inta committee with the uzbek ambassador to the eu, although he was invited repeatedly. i think it might have given us a glimpse of the situation inside. unfortunately, the bilateral meeting i was able to have with the ambassador was not very constructive either. on the other hand, i would like to thank my colleagues for being open to the concerns expressed by the european parliament and thank them for their valuable contribution to the final form. i believe that we have succeeded in obtaining a balanced report through which we ask the council to support the request of the ilo to uzbekistan to accept a high-level tripartite observer mission, with full freedom of movement, to assess the application of the ilo conventions. i would like to refer, finally, to the petition initiated by the anti-slavery organization calling for the end of trade preferences. last week i had the opportunity to meet some students from isbourne who came to the european parliament with members of anti-slavery to ask the european union to protect children's rights. and i must tell you, mr. president, that after this debate is over, i will be handing you a petition signed by 13,379 people asking for this.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i want to thank the honourable members for this very serious and important debate. let me focus on the course to suspend the generalised system of preferences (gsp preferences). on behalf of the commission i take note of the references made to the generalised system of preferences of which uzbekistan is currently a beneficiary. the gsp is an incentive-based tool to support development. its aim is to help developing countries to advance towards a better respect of international conventions on human and labour rights as well as to lock in essential reforms in these fields. the gsp preferences can be withdrawn from beneficiaries in cases of serious and systemic violations of the principles that are laid down in international instruments such as the core international labour organisation (ilo) conventions. we will continue to keep the situation under review, given that the legal conditions for suspension are not presently met, and we shall act accordingly. in the meantime, we will intensify the constructive dialogue we have with uzbekistan to help the ilo gain access to uzbek cotton fields. we very highly appreciate the cooperation with parliament in this regard.

author. − madam president, this is about an oral question and a motion for a resolution. what i would say about both the oral question and the joint motion for a resolution is that they put forward two basic propositions. firstly, that the restrictions for romanian and bulgarian workers on the european labour market should be lifted, as there is no real economic reason to keep them in place, and i quote here from a fresh report from the commission. secondly, the oral question and the motion for a resolution are asking for the states that want to exercise their right to extend the barriers to provide hard economic data in support of their request. since this whole debate was sometimes misunderstood or misrepresented, i have to state what the question and the motion for a resolution are not about. firstly, they are not about changing treaties or any other kind of legislation. they only ask for legislation to be implemented with good reason and not implemented at all when there is no reason. secondly, the question and the motion are not about encouraging vagueness. on the contrary, they propose more transparency, which is to say that from now on, member states should not be able to limit the fundamental rights of fellow european citizens by simply invoking a vague formula – by ticking a box. this sort of behaviour is neither rational nor legal: it is pure imposition. for those who wondered whether romanians and bulgarians could really not wait for another two years, the answer is no. when the issue is your rights, sometimes even a day can be too long. finally, the question and the motion push for full european consistency. i therefore have to ask: why maintain an arrangement that allows goods and capital to move freely towards east european member states while stopping east european citizens taking up jobs in western european countries?
author. − madam president, the right to live and work in another country of the union is one of the fundamental freedoms of the european union, and yet romanian and bulgarian workers face total or partial restrictions on their fundamental right of freedom of movement. transitional measures constitute a derogation from a fundamental freedom. those transitional measures are counter-productive in terms of combating forced self-employment, undeclared work and irregular employment. eleven member states still maintain partial or total restrictions, but this parliament still does not know how many of those have requested the extension of the transitional measures for the next two years. can the commission tell us how many requests it has received? can the commission also explain on what basis its judgment is going to be produced? at a time when racism, xenophobia and social conflict are increasing, it is of the utmost importance to guarantee social cohesion in the european union through effective integration policies promoting equal treatment, decent working conditions and social protection, and not to use derogations from fundamental freedoms as a political weapon. bulgarian and romanian citizens have the right to enjoy equal treatment just like other european citizens. this is also a way of ensuring fair competition between businesses and preventing any social and economic dumping. workers’ mobility in the european union should never be considered a threat to the internal labour market. therefore, our political groups support the opinion that all these transitional measures should be abolished.
member of the commission. − mr president, the free movement of workers is one of the fundamental freedoms, together with the free movement of goods, services and capital. it is a pillar of the single market and for 50 years it has contributed to making european integration a success. i know that the free movement of workers and the lifting of the restrictions in place are of significant importance to you and it is also important for the commission. as you know, the transitional arrangements aim at allowing member states to prepare gradually for the full application of eu law on the free movement of workers. the transitional arrangements were agreed for a maximum period of seven years, in three phases. each phase requires more and stronger justification from member states if they want to maintain the restriction to the free movement of workers. we are approaching the third and final phase of these seven years. in 2007, ten of the 25 other member states opened their labour markets for bulgarian and romanian workers immediately. by now, this number has increased for bulgarian workers to 15, and for romanian workers to 14 member states. even in the member states that still apply restrictions, several apply less strict conditions or simplified procedures in comparison to the conditions and procedures that applied to bulgarian and romanian workers prior to joining the eu. according to the transitional arrangements, a member states that currently still restricts the free movement of workers can only continue to do so for the final two years of the transitional period if it notifies the commission before 1 january 2012 of a serious disturbance of its labour market, or a threat thereof. this restriction can last until 31 december 2013 at the very latest. however, the transitional arrangements do not define what a serious disturbance of the labour market, or the threat thereof, is. as labour markets across the eu vary widely between member states, each member state will therefore have to assess itself whether it undergoes, or is threatened by, a serious labour market disturbance. the commission cannot lay down criteria that member states would have to use. the commission has made it clear though, that it expects any member state that wishes to extend restrictions on labour market access to explain why it considers it is undergoing or is threatened by a serious labour market disturbance and to provide justification with data and convincing, pertinent arguments when notifying the commission. as the commission stated in the report adopted on 11 november on the functioning of the transitional arrangements, it expects more than a simple reference to the unemployment rate. what is, however, important to remember is that the transitional arrangements do not stipulate that the serious labour market disturbance, or the threat thereof, must be caused by an influx of romanian and bulgarian workers. what is also important to note is that a member state only needs to send a notification within the deadline, without needing the commission’s assent to the notification. in that case national law on labour market access will continue to apply after 31 december 2011. concerning the disclosure of a letter of notification, the commission must, in accordance with existing procedures, consult in respect of each such request the member state from where the notification originates. in any case, the commission will check whether the notifications were sent within the deadline, which means before 1 january 2012. if not, eu law on free movement of workers will apply fully. at the employment, social policy, health and consumer affairs (epsco) council earlier this month, i encouraged governments to consider with great care, not only in light of the situation of the labour market, but also on the basis of the facts contained in the commission’s report, whether it is necessary to maintain restrictions on the labour market access of bulgarian and romanian workers. i reminded member states to keep in mind that the transitional arrangements aim at allowing member states to prepare gradually for the full application of eu law on free movement of workers and not at delaying its application until the very end of the transitional period. free movement of workers is one of the fundamental freedoms enshrined in the eu treaty and a strong symbol for all european citizens. apart from the right to work itself, working and living conditions are an important aspect here. bulgarian and romanian workers who have been admitted to work in a member state – even in ones that still apply restrictions – benefit fully from the provisions of eu law on free movement of workers that grant the right to equal treatment with nationals as regards conditions of employment and work, including pay. the labour market and social situation has been analysed in the commission report as well as in a specific chapter of the employment and social developments in europe review, a report to be adopted and presented on 15 december. however, as regards, ‘irregular’ bulgarian and romanian workers, the commission regrets that there is no detailed information or data about their number or social situation, which is precisely due to the hidden character of their presence in other member states. in its 2008 and 2011 reports on the functioning of transitional arrangements of bulgarian and romanian workers, the commission has already underlined that the restrictions to free movement of workers do not necessarily have the expected impact of protecting the national labour markets. in some cases, the restrictions can even exacerbate the incidence of undeclared work, leading to undesired social consequences both for undeclared workers and the regular labour force. the commission will continue to develop and promote, in relation with the member states, specific activities to fight undeclared work. finally, the posting of workers directive fully applies to bulgarian and romanian workers who are posted. it defines the core of mandatory working conditions to be respected in the host country by companies posting workers temporarily to that country, in particular with respect to maximum work periods and minimum rest periods; minimum paid annual holidays; the minimum rates of pay, and health and safety at work. the directive thus provides for a significant level of protection of posted workers and avoids that working conditions in the host country are undermined as an effect of competition. the commission is currently preparing a legislative proposal which will aim to improve and reinforce the implementation, application and enforcement in practice of the posting of workers directive. it will include measures to prevent and sanction any abuse and circumvention of the applicable rules. the adoption of the proposal is foreseen for february 2012. the incoming danish presidency will immediately start negotiations on this proposal.

a german company recently opened europe's largest solar park in eggebek, near the german border with denmark, and a romanian company installed the solar panels. the installation of over 400,000 solar panels was completed in just four months. the park has a capacity of 83 mw, covers an area of 3,2 km2 and the investment amounts to eur 130 million. the company in romania that placed the panels used a team of 250 workers, the vast majority from the arad municipality of tudor vladimirescu. the romanians installed on average over 3000 panels per day. such examples of skilled and highly skilled personnel from romania are numerous in the eu. i welcome germany's decision to change the criteria for access to the labour market, but i want all romanian and bulgarian citizens to enjoy free access to this market within the eu.
in two weeks, it will be five years since romania and bulgaria joined the european union. unfortunately, even after these five years, the two countries are not treated as equal partners within the european union. the romanian and bulgarian citizens are still being denied two fundamental freedoms, two european symbols, as commissioner andor has said, namely freedom of movement - by prohibiting accession to schengen - and the right to work freely in the european union. member states maintaining work restrictions for romanians and bulgarians do not intend to completely abandon them after 1 january 2012, although there is no objective basis to justify their extension. as the commission's reports prove, romanian and bulgarian workers have brought and continue to bring, not disruption, but important benefits to the economies of the countries in which they work. i think it is time for member states to decide whether or not they recognise equal membership in the european union for romania and bulgaria and whether or not they support the mobility of workers within the european union, as they have committed to in strategy 2020.

at the eu level, there are no 'our terms' and 'your terms', there are only the european union's terms. the free movement of persons is one of the fundamental freedoms guaranteed by the treaties, and this includes the right of union citizens to live and work in another member state. the contribution of migrant workers from the new member states to the development of the host economies is unanimously recognised. we demand the removal of barriers to the free movement of workers in romania and bulgaria and the respect of fundamental social rights for all workers. raising these barriers will protect migrant workers and host-country workers alike. the maintenance of these barriers creates conditions for social dumping and affects both host-country workers and migrant workers, who are forced to accept work below their level of training and with a salary lower than that of a native worker with the same skills. we call on the union and the member states to prevent the exploitation of migrant workers, to prevent the recruitment of migrants in precarious working and social protection conditions and to ensure access to education, health services and decent housing for migrant workers' families. the president agreed to answer a question by raising the 'blue card' (rule 149 (8) of the rules of procedure)

in writing. freedom of movement for workers is one of the basic principles of the functioning of the internal market. every community citizen has the freedom to seek employment, to work, to settle or to provide services in another member state. the european labour market can only function properly if this fundamental principle, enshrined in the european treaties, is respected. although there are currently many concrete initiatives in the eu to promote labour mobility, we can see that very few people are exercising this right. unfortunately, some member states have maintained restrictions on romanian and bulgarian nationals under the pretext of protecting the labour market against possible imbalances due to labour migration. several reports contradict the arguments made by these countries based on actual migration figures. it was thus confirmed that romanian and bulgarian workers have a positive impact on the eu economy. i believe that in the current global economic context, marked by a severe economic crisis, we have an obligation to support the removal of any barriers that are holding back the european economy and that have a negative effect on the level of labour mobility and the process of economic integration in general.

168 000 european citizens die each year as a result of accidents at work or occupational diseases, and another 7 million are injured in accidents at work. around 50% of workers in the european union do not have access to prevention services at work, particularly in smes and subcontracting chains. investments in occupational accident prevention policies ensure increased productivity and competitiveness, ensure viable social security systems and reduce social security expenditure, estimated at 5.9% of gdp. austerity measures during the economic crisis must not jeopardise health and safety measures. i would draw attention to the recognition of the harsh working conditions and the adoption of the health and safety measures necessary for this type of workplace. i believe that a gender perspective needs to be integrated into the policies of the european strategy 2007-2012 on health and safety at work to better reflect the specific risks faced by women at work.
in writing. – the european strategy 2007-2012 on health and safety at work ensures the fundamental right of eu citizens to have access to safe and favourable working conditions. while those in high-skilled positions enjoy a work environment that safeguards the health and safety of its employees, those in low-skilled and low-paying positions are subject to increased vulnerability as a result of illness, accidents and other work-related traumas. acknowledging the pervasiveness of precarious working conditions is the first step in challenging the status quo. a number of roadblocks exist, of course. undeclared labourers are arguably most at risk because of the informal agreement between them and their employers. they must be incentivised to guarantee the provision of a set of fair working conditions regardless of the skill level of their employees. like other member states, romania’s labour code explicitly provides for the protection of the health and safety of workers, yet applying it in practice remains a significant challenge.
member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to comment on two points: the crisis derogation and the specific renault case. as you know, the european globalisation adjustment fund is a new creation, but it was set up before the impact of the financial crisis on the labour markets of europe became clear. it became operational by 2007 but, at the end of 2008 (as was mentioned by the rapporteur), we changed the original substance of the fund, as a response to the redundancies among workers due to trade liberalisation and the impact of the globalisation of trade, and also to cover workers made redundant as a result of the financial crisis – and rightly so. this was part of a real anti-crisis response on behalf of the european institutions, increasing the co-financing rate on our side and extending the application of the fund. this was a key component of our anti-crisis response and also a political message of european solidarity. so far we have received 53 applications under the extended globalisation fund application, targeting more than 50 000 workers. but the crisis derogation was, by its nature, a temporary one and – as rightly explained by the rapporteur, ms matera – it will expire at the end of the month. as the crisis is not over, the commission wanted to extend the mandate to extend these derogations until the end of the present financial perspective – that is, until the end of 2013 – and, with the great responsibility here in this room, parliament adopted this proposal of extended derogation in september without any amendments. the council, on the other hand, has failed to extend the derogation, despite – i have to say, although it is not my role to praise the polish presidency – the efforts of the polish presidency. in practical terms this means the end of the derogation by the end of the year, although that is not the end of the crisis. all the data indicates that the unemployment rate in europe over the next two years will be not less than 10%. by blocking this proposal, a minority of member states – with the clear majority in favour of extending the crisis derogation – are putting an end to it. this means that the co-financing rate will come down to 50% and the scope of the globalisation fund will be limited to redundancies caused by trade globalisation. we already have in the pipeline ten new applications for the crisis derogation, affecting many thousands of people in europe. i am afraid that they may not be able to benefit from the scheme if it is not presented fully by the end of 2011. i must say that i disagree with some of the arguments used on this occasion by the member states creating a blocking minority in the council. the major one was that the problems of unemployment are better targeted at local level. there is a clear misunderstanding here, as the european globalisation fund is run by shared management, and the response must be designed locally by the member states and not in brussels. so this is a misunderstanding and not a real argument for ending the crisis derogations. there are also other arguments, which i think are not quite in touch with reality, for example that if we support redundant workers, this will relieve the member states of a sense of responsibility. but it is co-financing, and if we see clearly in the statistics that the rich states are better utilising the globalisation fund, that means a real problem of co-financing and sharing responsibility – also financial responsibility – on the part of a member state. i also have to say – because this is a clear support of the globalisation fund – that so far more than 40% of the workers made redundant due to the crisis but covered by the globalisation fund have been able to find another job, so this is working. this is simply working to enhance the labour markets of europe. but, in practical terms, we have no more crisis derogation in 2012, and i think this is a wrong political message to send to the labour markets: but what can we do? we can only encourage applications under the original trade globalisation criteria, and this is what the commission can do under the present circumstances. i have one further, short comment, as this is a joint debate on the specific renault case. we are taking into consideration the issue, raised by several honourable members of the european parliament, of the ex-renault workers who left the company to join the early retirement scheme and were subsequently negatively affected by the reform of the french pension system. of course we take their fate into account and are in touch with renault in order to address the issue. the renault company has committed itself to taking the necessary measures to ensure that those concerned will not be disregarded and to keep the commission informed of their actions, but legally the issue has nothing to do with the mobilisation of the european globalisation fund. this is a human issue but is not legally an issue of the mobilisation of the european globalisation fund, as the workers leaving for the early retirement scheme were not targeted for globalisation fund support. france still has four months to prepare and submit a complete report on the implementation of its measures to handle the fate of the workers. the commission, for our part, reserves the right to carry out an audit to check that the globalisation fund application – and this is in the scope of our responsibility – was properly spent. so here is the role of the commission. from the legal point of view, the question is whether the requirements for the globalisation fund are fulfilled by the renault application. ms matera is saying yes, i know, but this is the legal case. the commission shares the review with the council. renault has made more than 500 workers (this is one of the criteria) redundant as a direct consequence of the global financial crisis. our contribution (within the nature of the globalisation fund) is to be used to co-finance active labour market policy measures. so the only reasonable conclusion today is that the globalisation fund should be mobilised and should contribute in full the amount requested by france. thank you for listening to both the specific points on derogation and the specific renault case.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, thank you very much, mr schwab, for your good work in making this report on our 2010 competition policy report. i would also like to thank the rapporteurs of the other committees of this parliament, such as the committee on the internal market and consumer protection and the committee on transport and tourism, who have also contributed to this report. in the 2010 competition policy report, the commission gives an account of its activities, as it does every year; as mr schwab says, 40 reports already on the development of a policy central to the completion of the internal market and the creation of conditions for economic growth, innovation and, in general, the progress of our economies, always thinking - and i agree with what mr schwab said - of citizens as consumers of goods or as users of services: these are the final recipients of competition policy. we are developing competition policy in times of crisis, and i agree with mr schwab's view, and we discussed this recently in the committee on economic and monetary affairs when i presented the commission's work programme for 2012 in this area: competition policy must take account of the fact that we are in crisis, but it must not be weaker because we are in crisis or in the fight against cartels, where, of course, we must continue to be extremely rigorous, either in politics, in the actions against abuses of dominant positions in the market. in difficult times it is much more harmful for businesses and for all citizens that there are those who abuse their power in the market to obtain particular advantages to the detriment of other competitors and to the detriment of consumers. we must remain vigilant about the possible risks to competition from mergers and acquisitions, which are starting to revive because there is a lot of liquidity in companies, in funds, inside and outside the european union, and there are asset purchase prices and company purchase prices that have fallen as a result of the crisis and that are creating opportunities. we are therefore still active in all areas of the policy to combat cartels, abuse of dominant positions and merger and acquisition control, especially as we are in a crisis. and of course, as mr schwab has said, the control of state aid, of public aid, is fundamental. public aid in times of crisis increases - and i will now refer specifically to aid to the financial system - but aid to the non-financial sectors has also increased in years of crisis, and we have had a specific time frame for controlling state aid in times of crisis which has prevented protectionist temptations from materializing and has prevented barriers from being created in the internal market as a result of the defensive use of public aid to protect companies in one country against the rest of the countries of the european union. that framework for state aid is currently facing a limit in most member states, which is that, subject as they are to very strict fiscal consolidation programmes, they have to prioritise much better and much more carefully the use of their public funds and therefore we should not encourage them from the state aid regulation to spend more, but we should be strict in the control of state aid so that they spend better and fine-tune their priorities better. resources are scarcer in the public coffers and the need to foster those activities with a future, those activities that must pull our economies and move towards a model of sustainable, inclusive growth, compatible with our environmental goals, is key. and finally, aid to the financial system. as mr schwab said, since the beginning of the crisis in 2007, but especially since the collapse of lehman brothers in september 2008, we have been faced with a dilemma: either we authorise exceptional aid to the financial system or the financial system collapses. and the collapse of the financial system would have meant the freezing of our economic activities; we cannot sustain economic activity without a sound functioning of the financial system. but this public aid, in terms of guarantees and guarantees, but also in terms of injections of public capital into a number of financial institutions or in terms of support for liquidity or for the treatment of damaged assets, has reached a more than considerable volume. the commission, through me as commissioner for competition, has sent this parliament a document, a study not only of the size of this aid but also of its impact until the end of 2010 - which i hope will be able to be supplemented in the coming months by what has happened in 2011 - aid to the financial system which, in general terms, has been translated into around 9-10 points of gdp in guarantees or guarantees offered by the member states in support of the financial system. it must be said that in only one case, so far, have these guarantees and guarantees had to be given; in the other cases it is a risk, but a risk which has not been given and which allows the member states, in the meantime, to receive revenue for providing this protection, this guarantee. some 3% of european gdp has been channelled to financial institutions in terms of public capital. the return of public capital has begun, but there are still very important financial institutions in several eu countries where the state has had to take part in its capital - assuming obvious risks - and there is 1% of gdp allocated to public resources for the treatment of damaged assets. i wanted to have put an end to this special system, exceptional in times of crisis, now, at the end of this year. unfortunately, with the new tensions that have been recorded in the financial markets since the summer, since the month of august, this is impossible. we need to continue with this exceptional framework, this exceptional regime of public support for the financial system in times of crisis. i hope that in a few months, before the end of 2012, i will be able to come to this house and announce to you that this system is no longer necessary but, in the meantime, it will be necessary with the adaptations we have included. what i can say again and again, what i have already said in this house and on several occasions in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, is that the rigour with which we monitor such aid, the demands in return for aid in terms of restructuring the entities benefiting from it, in terms of proper burden-sharing between all the parties benefiting from it, and the setting of requirements and requirements so that no further distortions are created in our internal market as a result of such aid, those three principles are still present, even more so than ever as the need for such treatment in times of crisis especially extends over more than three years. that's what i wanted to tell you. i thank again mr schwab, his colleagues in other committees, the members of this parliament for the work they have done on this report. and finally, i agree with mr schwab that the report, as from the next edition, will be, as we have discussed with him and his colleagues, a more synthetic report on everything that is already known by other means. we will not repeat in the report information that is available in real time through the websites or previous information. we shall focus the report more closely on those issues which merit special analysis and discussion because, as you know, although many decisions in competition policy are the exclusive competence of the commission, my intention from the beginning - and will remain so until the end - is to keep this parliament permanently associated and in constant dialogue with the commission so that the competition
